chapters.title: Letter of Dedication
paragraphs:
TO THE MOST WISE AND ILLUSTRIOUS THE DEAN AND DOCTORS OF THE SACRED FACULTY OF THEOLOGY OF PARIS.

GENTLEMEN,

1. I am so confident that, once you learn its aim, you will also agree that my reason for presenting this Treatise to you is a sound one, and that there is good ground for you to take it under your protection, that the best way I can recommend it to you is to state briefly the end I set myself in writing it.

2. I have always held that the two questions about God and the Soul are the chief ones to be settled with the help of Philosophy rather than Theology. For us who are faithful, it is enough to hold as matters of faith that the human soul does not perish with the body and that God exists. Yet it certainly seems impossible ever to persuade infidels of the reality of any religion, or almost even of any moral virtue, unless those two things are first proved to them by natural reason. And since this life often holds out greater rewards for vice than for virtue, few would prefer the right to the useful if neither the fear of God nor the expectation of another life restrained them. It is quite true that we must believe God exists because the sacred Scriptures teach it, and that, on the other hand, we must believe the sacred Scriptures because they come from God. (For faith is a gift of God, so the same Being who gives the grace to believe other things can also give the grace to believe his own existence.) Nevertheless, this cannot be put to infidels, who would think the reasoning went in a circle. Indeed, I have observed that you, along with all the other theologians, not only affirmed that natural reason is sufficient to prove the existence of God, but also that sacred Scripture lets us infer that the knowledge of God is much clearer than the knowledge of many created things, and so easy to acquire that those who lack it are to blame. This is manifest from these words of the Book of Wisdom, chap. xiii., where it is said, Howbeit they are not to be excused; for if their understanding was so great that they could discern the world and the creatures, why did they not rather find out the Lord thereof? And in Romans, chap. i., it is said that they are without excuse; and again, in the same place, by these words, That which may be known of God is manifest in them — we seem to be admonished that all that can be known of God can be made manifest by reasons drawn from no other source than the inspection of our own minds. I have therefore thought it would not be unbecoming for me to inquire how, and by what way, without going out of ourselves, God may be known more easily and certainly than the things of the world.

3. As for the Soul, many have judged that its nature cannot easily be discovered, and some have even ventured to say that human reason leads to the conclusion that it perishes with the body, and that the contrary opinion can be held through faith alone. Nevertheless, the Lateran Council, held under Leo X. (in session viii.), condemns these people and expressly orders Christian philosophers to refute their arguments and to establish the truth to the best of their ability. So I have ventured to attempt this in the present work.

4. Moreover, I know that most of the irreligious deny the existence of God and the distinctness of the human soul from the body for no other reason than that, as they allege, these points have never yet been demonstrated. I am by no means of their opinion. On the contrary, I hold that almost all the proofs which great men have offered on these questions have, when rightly understood, the force of demonstrations, and that it is next to impossible to discover new ones. Yet I think there is no more useful service to be done in Philosophy than for someone, once for all, to seek out the best of these reasons carefully and set them out so accurately and clearly that, from then on, it would be manifest to all that they are real demonstrations. Finally, many persons greatly wanted this. They knew that I had cultivated a certain Method of resolving all kinds of difficulties in the sciences. It is not indeed new (there being nothing older than truth), but they were aware that I had used it successfully in other instances. So I judged it my duty to try it on the present matter as well.

5. This Treatise contains the sum of what I have managed to accomplish on the subject. I did not try to gather every reason that could be offered as a proof here, since that seems necessary only where no single proof of adequate certainty is available. I dealt only with the first and chief ones, and in such a way that I would now venture to put them forward as demonstrations of the highest certainty and evidence. I will add that I am led to think no way lies open to the human mind of ever discovering better proofs. The importance of the subject, and the glory of God, to which it all relates, constrain me to speak here somewhat more freely about myself than I have been accustomed to do. Nevertheless, whatever certitude and evidence I may find in these demonstrations, I cannot therefore persuade myself that they are within the comprehension of all. Take geometry. It has many demonstrations by Archimedes, Apollonius, Pappus and others. Everyone accepts them as evident and even certain, because, considered by itself, each manifestly contains nothing that is not very easy to understand, and no consequents that are inaccurately related to their antecedents. Yet very few people understand them, because they are somewhat long and demand the reader's whole attention. In the same way, I consider the demonstrations I use here to be equal or even superior to the geometrical in certitude and evidence, and I am afraid that many will nevertheless fail to understand them adequately. They too are somewhat long and involved. But chiefly, they require a mind entirely free from prejudice, one that can easily detach itself from the commerce of the senses. And, to speak the truth, fewer people have a gift for metaphysical studies than for geometry. There is, besides, a further difference. In geometry everyone is persuaded that nothing is usually put forward without a certain demonstration. So those who are only partly versed in it more often go wrong by assenting to what is false, out of a desire to seem to understand it, than by denying what is true. In philosophy, on the other hand, where everything is believed to be doubtful, few give themselves sincerely to the search after truth. By far the greater number seek a reputation as bold thinkers by audaciously attacking the most weighty truths.

6. Hence, whatever force my reasonings may have, I do not expect them to move the minds of men much, because they belong to philosophy, unless you give them your patronage and approval. But your Faculty is held in such great esteem by all, and the name of SORBONNE carries such authority, that no other society, after the Sacred Councils, has had its judgment so deferred to, in matters of faith and even in human philosophy. Everyone is convinced that nowhere else can greater perspicacity and solidity be found, or greater wisdom and integrity in judging. So I do not doubt the following. Suppose you will condescend to give this Treatise enough regard to be willing, first, to correct it (for, mindful not only of my humanity but chiefly of my ignorance, I do not affirm that it is free from errors); second, to supply what it lacks, complete what is unfinished, and give fuller illustration where this is called for, or at least to point out these defects to me so that I may endeavor to remedy them; and finally, once its reasonings for the existence of God and for the distinction of the human soul from the body have been brought to such perspicuity that they are esteemed exact demonstrations (and I am assured they can be), you will condescend to grant them the authority of your approbation and give public testimony of their truth and certainty. Then I do not doubt, I say, that all the errors ever entertained on these questions will very soon be effaced from the minds of men. For truth itself will readily lead the rest of the ingenious and the learned to subscribe to your judgment. Your authority will make the atheists, who are in general smatterers rather than ingenious or learned, lay aside the spirit of contradiction. It will lead them, perhaps, to do battle in their own persons for reasonings which they find all men of genius considering demonstrations, lest they should seem not to understand them. Finally, the rest of mankind will readily trust so many testimonies, and no one will venture any longer to doubt either the existence of God or the real distinction of mind and body. You, in your singular wisdom, are the ones to judge how important it is to establish such beliefs, [who are cognizant of the disorders which doubt of these truths produces].* But it would not become me here to commend the cause of God and of religion any further to you, who have always proved the strongest support of the Catholic Church.

chapters.title: Preface to the Reader
paragraphs: 1. I have already touched slightly on the questions about the existence of God and the nature of the human soul in the 'Discourse on the Method of rightly conducting the Reason, and seeking Truth in the Sciences,' published in French in the year 1637. I did not intend to treat them fully there, but only, as it were, in passing, so that I could learn from my readers' judgment how I should handle them afterward. These questions seemed to me important enough to be considered more than once. The path I follow in discussing them is so little trodden, and so far from the ordinary route, that I thought it inadvisable to illustrate it at greater length in French, in a discourse that could be read by all, lest even the feebler minds should believe that they could enter upon this path.

2. In the 'Discourse on Method' I asked everyone who might find anything deserving censure in my writings to do me the favor of pointing it out to me. I may state that, apart from two, no objections worthy of remark have been raised against what I then said on these questions. I will reply briefly to these two here, before undertaking the more detailed discussion.

3. The first objection runs as follows. While the human mind reflects on itself, it perceives nothing about itself except that it is a thinking thing. But it does not follow that its nature or essence consists only in being a thing which thinks, if the word ONLY is to exclude everything else that might perhaps also be said to belong to the nature of the mind. My reply is that in that place I did not mean to exclude such things according to the order of truth in the matter (which I did not then treat), but only according to the order of thought (perception). What I meant was this: so far as I was conscious, I clearly apprehended nothing else as belonging to my essence than that I was a thinking thing, or a thing having in itself the faculty of thinking. I will show hereafter how it follows, from the consciousness that nothing besides thinking belongs to the essence of the mind, that nothing else does in truth belong to it.

4. The second objection runs: I possess the idea of a thing more perfect than I am, but it does not follow that the idea itself is more perfect than I am, and much less that what it represents exists. My reply is that the term idea is equivocal here. Taken materially, it means an act of the understanding, and in that sense it cannot be said to be more perfect than I. Taken objectively, it means the thing which that act represents. Even if this thing is not supposed to exist outside my understanding, it may still be more perfect than I am, by reason of its essence. Later in this treatise I will show more fully how the existence of this thing follows from my possessing the idea of a thing more perfect than myself.

5. Apart from these two objections, I have seen two fairly long treatises on this matter. They attacked my conclusions, much more than my premises, and did so with arguments borrowed from the commonplaces of the atheists. Such arguments cannot impress those who rightly understand my reasonings. Many people judge so weakly and irrationally that the opinions first presented to them on a subject persuade them more than a true and solid refutation that arrives later, however false and contrary to reason those first opinions are. For that reason I am unwilling to reply to these strictures here, since I dread being obliged to state them first. I will say only this in general. Whatever the atheists commonly allege against the existence of God always comes from one of two things: either they ascribe human affections to Deity, or they attribute so much vigor and wisdom to our minds that we presume to determine and comprehend both what God can do and what he ought to do. So none of their allegations need trouble us, provided only that we remember that our minds must be considered finite, while Deity is incomprehensible and infinite.

6. Having now tested, in some measure, how men receive my work, I take up God and the human soul once more, and with them the principles of the entire First Philosophy. I expect no praise from the crowd for my endeavors, and no wide circle of readers. On the contrary, I advise no one to read this work except those who are able and willing to meditate with me in earnest, to detach their minds from commerce with the senses, and to deliver themselves from all prejudice. People of that character are, I well know, remarkably rare. Others do not care to grasp the order and connection of the reasonings. They study only isolated clauses, in order to carp noisily over small points, as many do. I may say that such persons will gain little from reading this treatise. They may perhaps find occasion for cavilling in several places, but they will hardly raise any pressing objection, or any that deserves a reply.

7. Now, I do not promise to satisfy others on all these subjects at first sight. Nor do I presume so much as to believe that I could foresee everything that might trouble each reader. So I shall begin by setting out in the Meditations the considerations through which I feel persuaded that I have reached a certain and evident knowledge of truth. I want to find out whether the reasonings that have prevailed with me will also be effective in convincing others. After that I will reply to the objections of certain men, illustrious for their genius and learning, to whom these Meditations were sent for criticism before they went to press. Their objections are so numerous and varied that I venture to expect nothing, or at least nothing of any moment, will readily occur to any mind that they have not touched upon. For this reason I earnestly entreat my readers to form no judgment on the questions raised in the Meditations until they have taken care to read the whole of the Objections, with the relative Replies.

chapters.title: Synopsis of the Six Following Meditations
paragraphs: 1. In the First Meditation I set out the grounds on which we may doubt of all things in general, and especially of material objects, so long at least as we have no other foundations for the sciences than those we have had until now. Although the usefulness of so general a doubt may not be manifest at first sight, it is nevertheless of the greatest. It delivers us from all prejudice, and affords the easiest pathway by which the mind may withdraw itself from the senses. And finally, it makes it impossible for us to doubt anything we afterward discover to be true.

2. In the Second, the mind uses the freedom that belongs to it alone to suppose that nothing exists of whose existence it has the slightest doubt. It finds that, meanwhile, it must itself exist. This too is a point of the highest moment, since it lets the mind easily distinguish what belongs to itself, that is, to the intellectual nature, from what is to be referred to the body. Some, perhaps, will expect at this stage a statement of the reasons which establish the doctrine of the immortality of the soul. I think it proper to make such readers aware that I aimed to write nothing of which I could not give exact demonstration. So I felt obliged to follow an order like that of the geometers, viz., to premise everything on which the proposition in question depends before drawing any conclusion about it. The first and chief prerequisite for knowing the immortality of the soul is to form the clearest possible conception (conceptus—concept) of the soul itself, absolutely distinct from all our notions of body; there I show how this is done. We need, besides, the assurance that all objects which we clearly and distinctly think are true (really exist) in just the mode in which we think them; this could not be established before the Fourth Meditation. We must also, for the same purpose, have a distinct conception of corporeal nature, which is given partly in the Second and partly in the Fifth and Sixth Meditations. Finally, on these grounds, we are compelled to conclude that all objects clearly and distinctly conceived as diverse substances, as mind and body are, really are substances distinct from each other; this inference is made in the Sixth Meditation. This Second Meditation also confirms the absolute distinction of mind and body, by showing that body can be conceived only as divisible, whereas mind can be conceived only as indivisible. We cannot conceive half of a mind, as we can half of any body, however small. So the natures of these two substances must be held to be not only diverse but even, in some measure, contraries. I have not pursued this discussion further in the present treatise, for two reasons. First, these considerations suffice to show that the destruction of the mind does not follow from the corruption of the body, and so to give men the hope of a future life. Second, the premises from which the immortality of the soul can be inferred involve an explanation of the whole principles of Physics. In the first place, we would have to establish that all substances generally, that is, all things which can exist only because God created them, are incorruptible in their own nature and can never cease to be, unless God himself reduces them to nothing by withdrawing his concurrence. In the second place, we would have to establish that body, taken generally, is a substance, and therefore can never perish. The human body, in so far as it differs from other bodies, is constituted only by a certain configuration of members and other accidents of this sort. The human mind, by contrast, is not made up of accidents but is a pure substance. For even if all the accidents of the mind change — if, for example, it thinks certain things, wills others, and perceives others — the mind itself does not vary with these changes. The human body, on the contrary, is no longer the same once the form of any of its parts changes. From this it follows that the body may indeed perish without difficulty, but that the mind is in its own nature immortal.

3. In the Third Meditation I have set out, at sufficient length as it seems to me, my chief argument for the existence of God. But there I wanted to avoid comparisons taken from material objects, in order to withdraw my readers' minds from the senses as far as possible. So numerous obscurities perhaps remain, which I trust will afterward be removed entirely in the Replies to the Objections. For example, it may be difficult to understand, among other things, how the idea of a being absolutely perfect, which is found in our minds, has so much objective reality [i. e., participates by representation in so many degrees of being and perfection] that it must be held to arise from a cause absolutely perfect. The Replies illustrate this with the comparison of a highly perfect machine, whose idea exists in the mind of some workman. This idea has objective (i.e.., representative) perfection, and that perfection must have some cause, viz, either the workman's science or that of some other person from whom he received the idea. In the same way, the idea of God which is found in us demands God himself for its cause.

4. The Fourth shows that everything we clearly and distinctly perceive (apprehend) is true, and at the same time explains what the nature of error consists in. We need to know these points, both to confirm the preceding truths and to understand better those that follow. Meanwhile, it must be observed that there I do not treat of Sin at all, that is, of error committed in pursuing good and evil, but only of the kind of error that arises in determining what is true and what is false. Nor do I refer to matters of faith or the conduct of life, but only to speculative truths, those known by the natural light alone.

5. The Fifth illustrates corporeal nature taken generically, and it also gives a new demonstration of the existence of God. This demonstration is perhaps no more free than the former from certain difficulties, but their solution will be found in the Replies to the Objections. I further show in what sense it is true that even the certitude of geometrical demonstrations depends on the knowledge of God.

6. Finally, in the Sixth, the act of the understanding (intellectio) is distinguished from the act of the imagination (imaginatio), and the marks of this distinction are described. The human mind is shown to be really distinct from the body, and yet so closely joined to it that the two form, as it were, a unity. All the errors that arise from the senses are reviewed, and the means of avoiding them are pointed out. Finally, I bring forward all the grounds from which the existence of material objects may be inferred. I do not do this because I thought them very useful for establishing what they prove, viz., that there is in reality a world, that men have bodies, and the like, which no one of sound mind ever seriously doubted. I do it because a close consideration of them shows that they are neither so strong nor so clear as the reasonings that lead us to the knowledge of our mind and of God. Thus the latter are the most certain and manifest of everything that can come under human knowledge — a conclusion which it was my single aim in these Meditations to establish. For that reason I omit here the various other questions which I also had occasion to consider in the course of the discussion.

chapters.title: Meditation 1 — Of the Things of Which We May Doubt
paragraphs: 1. Several years ago I became aware that, from my youth on, I had accepted many false opinions as true, and that whatever I had built on them afterward was therefore highly doubtful. I concluded that I had to rid myself, once in my life, of all the opinions I had taken in, and start again from the foundation, if I wanted to establish anything firm and lasting in the sciences. But the task seemed enormous, so I waited until I reached an age so mature that no later stage of life could offer me any better hope of carrying out my plan. That is why I have put it off for so long. I would now be doing wrong if I spent in deliberation any of the time that remains for action. Today, then, I have conveniently freed my mind from all cares [and am happily troubled by no passions], and I have secure leisure in a peaceful retreat. So at last I will turn earnestly and freely to the general overthrow of all my former opinions.

2. To do this, I do not need to show that every one of these opinions is false. That is a point I may perhaps never reach. My reason already convinces me that I should withhold belief from what is not entirely certain and indubitable just as carefully as from what is plainly false. So it will be enough to justify rejecting them all if I find some ground for doubt in each. Nor do I need to go through the beliefs one by one, which would be truly endless labor. When the foundation is removed from below, the whole building necessarily falls. So I will go straight to examining the principles on which all my former beliefs rested.

3. Everything I have accepted up to now as most true and certain, I received from the senses or through them. But I have observed that the senses sometimes mislead us, and prudence says never to place absolute confidence in what has deceived us even once.

4. But someone may say that the senses occasionally mislead us about small objects, or about things too far away to examine closely, yet many other things they report (presentations) cannot manifestly be doubted. For example, that I am in this place, seated by the fire, wearing a winter dressing gown, holding this piece of paper in my hands, and other things of the same kind. But how could I deny that these hands and this body are mine? I would have to count myself among the insane, whose brains are so disordered and clouded by dark bilious vapors that they stubbornly insist they are kings when they are in the greatest poverty, or that they are dressed [in gold] and purple when they have nothing on, or that their head is made of clay, their body of glass, or that they are gourds. But these people are madmen, and I would be no less insane than they if I took such extravagant examples as my guide.

5. This is true, but I must still consider that I am a man, and so I am in the habit of sleeping and of picturing to myself in dreams the same things the insane imagine when awake, or sometimes even less probable things. How often have I dreamt that I was in these familiar circumstances, that I was dressed and sitting here by the fire, when I was actually lying undressed in bed? At this moment, though, I certainly look at this paper with eyes wide awake. The head I am moving is not asleep. I stretch out this hand knowingly and on purpose, and I perceive it. Events in sleep are not so distinct as all this. But I cannot forget that at other times I have been deceived in sleep by similar illusions. When I consider those cases attentively, I perceive so clearly that there are no certain marks by which waking can ever be told apart from sleep that I am greatly astonished. In my amazement I almost persuade myself that I am dreaming now.

6. Let us suppose, then, that we are dreaming, and that all these particulars — the opening of the eyes, the motion of the head, the stretching out of the hands — are mere illusions. Let us suppose even that we really have neither an entire body nor hands such as we see. Nevertheless, we must at least admit that the things appearing to us in sleep are, as it were, painted representations, and that these could not have been formed except in the likeness of realities. Therefore, at the very least, those general things — eyes, a head, hands, and an entire body — are not simply imaginary but really exist. For even painters, when they try to represent sirens and satyrs in the most fantastic and extraordinary forms, cannot give them entirely new natures. They can only make a medley of the limbs of different animals. And if they happen to imagine something so new that nothing like it has ever been seen, and which is therefore purely fictitious and absolutely false, still the colors it is made of must be real. By the same principle, although these general things, namely [a body], eyes, a head, hands and the like, may be imaginary, we are nevertheless absolutely compelled to admit the reality of some other things still simpler and more universal. Just as the painter's colors are real, so these are the things from which all the images of things in our consciousness (cogitatio) are formed, whether those images are true and real or false and fantastic.

7. To this class of things seem to belong corporeal nature in general and its extension; the figure of extended things; their quantity or magnitude, and their number; also the place in which they exist, the time during which they last, and other things of the same sort.

8. So we will perhaps not reason wrongly if we conclude from this that Physics, Astronomy, Medicine, and all the other sciences that study composite things are indeed of doubtful character. But Arithmetic, Geometry, and the other sciences of the same kind, which deal only with the simplest and most general things and hardly ask whether they really exist, contain something certain and indubitable. For whether I am awake or dreaming, two and three make five, and a square has only four sides. It does not seem possible that truths so apparent could ever come under suspicion of falsity [or uncertainty].

9. Nevertheless, the belief that there is an all-powerful God who created me, such as I am, has long held firm possession of my mind. How, then, do I know that he has not arranged for there to be no earth, no sky, no extended thing, no figure, no magnitude, no place, while still providing [that I have the perceptions of all these things, and] the persuasion that they exist in just the way I perceive them? Further, I sometimes think that others are in error about matters they believe they know perfectly. How do I know that I am not deceived in the same way each time I add two and three, or count the sides of a square, or form some judgment still simpler, if anything simpler can be imagined? But perhaps God has not been willing for me to be deceived in this way, for he is said to be supremely good. Yet if it were contrary to the goodness of Deity to have created me subject to constant deception, it would seem equally contrary to his goodness to allow me to be deceived even occasionally. And it is clear that this is permitted.

10. Some people, indeed, might perhaps be found who would rather deny the existence of so powerful a Being than believe that nothing is certain. But for the present let us not oppose this view, and let us grant that everything said here about a Deity is fable. Still, however it is supposed that I came to be what I am, whether by fate, or chance, or an endless series of antecedents and consequents, or any other means, being deceived and being in error are a certain defect. So it is clear that the probability of my being so imperfect as to be constantly deceived increases exactly as the power of the cause assigned as my origin decreases. To these arguments I have assuredly nothing to reply. I am forced at last to admit that there is nothing among all I formerly believed true that it is impossible to doubt, and this not through thoughtlessness or levity but for cogent and carefully considered reasons. So from now on, if I want to discover anything certain, I should withhold assent from those same opinions just as carefully as from what could be shown to be manifestly false.

11. But it is not enough to have made these observations. I must also take care to remember them. For those old, customary opinions keep coming back. Long and familiar use gives them the right to occupy my mind, even almost against my will, and to take control of my belief. I will not lose the habit of deferring to them and trusting them so long as I consider them what they truly are, namely, opinions that are to some extent doubtful, as I have already shown, but still highly probable, and that it is much more reasonable to believe than to deny. For this reason I am persuaded that I will not be doing wrong if, deliberately taking the opposite judgment, I become my own deceiver. I will suppose for a time that all those opinions are entirely false and imaginary, until at length I have balanced my old prejudices against my new ones, and my judgment is no longer turned aside by distorted habit from the path that may lead to the perception of truth. For I am assured that in the meantime this course will bring neither danger nor error, and that I cannot for now yield too much to distrust, since the end I am seeking is not action but knowledge.

12. I will suppose, then, not that God, who is supremely good and the fountain of truth, but that some malignant demon, who is at once exceedingly potent and deceitful, has used all his artifice to deceive me. I will suppose that the sky, the air, the earth, colors, figures, sounds, and all external things are nothing but the illusions of dreams, by which this being has laid snares for my credulity. I will consider myself as having no hands, eyes, flesh, blood, or any senses, and as falsely believing that I have them. I will stay resolutely fixed in this belief. If by this means it is not in my power to arrive at knowledge of truth, I shall at least do what is in my power, namely, [suspend my judgment], and guard with firm purpose against assenting to what is false and being imposed upon by this deceiver, however great his power and artifice. But this undertaking is arduous, and a certain laziness gradually leads me back to my ordinary way of life. A captive, perhaps enjoying an imaginary liberty in his dreams, begins to suspect that it is only a vision. He dreads waking up, and goes along with the pleasant illusions so that the deception may last longer. In the same way I, of my own accord, fall back into my former beliefs, and I am afraid to wake from my slumber. I fear that the laborious wakefulness following this quiet rest, instead of bringing any daylight, will not be enough to dispel the darkness raised by the difficulties I have now brought up.

chapters.title: Meditation 2 — Of the Nature of the Human Mind, And That It Is More Easily Known Than the Body
paragraphs: 1. Yesterday's Meditation has filled my mind with so many doubts that I can no longer forget them. Nor do I yet see any principle by which they can be resolved. It is as if I had suddenly fallen into very deep water. I am so thrown off balance that I can neither plant my feet on the bottom nor keep myself up by swimming. Nevertheless, I will make an effort and try again the path I entered yesterday. That is, I will set aside everything that admits of the slightest doubt, just as if I had found it to be absolutely false. I will keep to this track until I find something certain, or at least, if I can do nothing more, until I know with certainty that nothing is certain. Archimedes asked for only one firm and immovable point in order to move the whole globe from its place to another. In the same way, I am entitled to the highest expectations if I am fortunate enough to find even one thing that is certain and indubitable.

2. I suppose, accordingly, that everything I see is false (fictitious). I believe that none of the things my deceptive memory represents ever existed. I suppose that I have no senses. I believe that body, figure, extension, motion and place are only fictions of my mind. What, then, can be considered true? Perhaps only this: that there is absolutely nothing certain.

3. But how do I know that there is not something entirely different from the things I have just listed, something about which it is impossible to have the slightest doubt? Is there not a God, or some being, whatever name I give him, who causes these thoughts to arise in my mind? But why suppose such a being, when I myself may be able to produce them? Am I, then, at least something? But I have just denied that I have senses or a body. I hesitate, however, for what follows from that? Am I so dependent on the body and the senses that I cannot exist without them? But I was persuaded that there was absolutely nothing in the world: no sky, no earth, no minds, no bodies. Was I not, then, also persuaded that I did not exist? Far from it. I certainly existed, since I was persuaded. But there is I know not what being, supremely powerful and deeply cunning, who constantly uses all his ingenuity to deceive me. Doubtless, then, I exist, since I am deceived. And let him deceive me as much as he can, he will never bring it about that I am nothing, as long as I am conscious that I am something. So, after weighing everything fully and carefully, I must finally conclude that this proposition (pronunciatum) I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time I express it or conceive it in my mind.

4. But I do not yet know clearly enough what I am, though I am sure that I am. So, next, I must take care not to carelessly put some other object in the place of myself, and so go astray even in that knowledge (cognition) which I hold to be the most certain and evident of all. For this reason I will now consider again what I used to believe myself to be, before I began this train of thought. From that earlier opinion I will remove everything that the grounds of doubt I have given could weaken even slightly, so that in the end nothing remains but what is certain and indubitable.

5. What, then, did I formerly think I was? I judged, of course, that I was a man. But what is a man? Shall I say a rational animal? Certainly not. I would then have to ask what is meant by animal, and what by rational. From a single question I would slip, without noticing, into others, and harder ones than the first. Nor do I now have enough leisure to waste on subtleties of this kind. I prefer to attend here to the thoughts that arose of themselves in my mind, inspired by my own nature alone, when I set myself to consider what I was. First, then, I thought I had a face, hands, arms, and the whole structure of limbs that is seen in a corpse, and I called this by the name of body. It also occurred to me that I was nourished, that I walked, perceived and thought, and I referred all these actions to the soul. But what the soul itself was, I either did not stop to consider, or, if I did, I imagined it to be something extremely rare and subtle, like wind, or flame, or ether, spread through my grosser parts. As for the body, I had no doubt about its nature. I thought I knew it distinctly, and if I had wanted to describe it according to the notions I then held, I would have put it this way. By body I understand whatever can be bounded by a certain figure; whatever can be contained in a certain place and so fill a space as to exclude every other body from it; whatever can be perceived by touch, sight, hearing, taste or smell; and whatever can be moved in various ways, not by itself but by something else that touches it [and from which it receives the impression]. For I held that the power to move itself, like the power to perceive and to think, did not belong at all to the nature of body. On the contrary, I was somewhat astonished to find such faculties in some bodies.

6. But [as for myself, what can I now say that I am], since I suppose there is an extremely powerful and, if I may say so, malignant being whose whole effort is directed to deceiving me? Can I affirm that I have any one of the attributes I have just described as belonging to the nature of body? I consider them attentively in my own mind, and I find none of them that can properly be said to belong to me. To list them would be idle and tedious. Let us pass, then, to the attributes of the soul. The first named were nutrition and walking. But if it is true that I have no body, it is also true that I can neither walk nor be nourished. Perception is another attribute of the soul. But perception too is impossible without the body. Besides, I have often believed in sleep that I perceived things which I afterward saw I had not really perceived. Thinking is another attribute of the soul, and here I find what properly belongs to me. This alone cannot be separated from me. I am — I exist: this is certain. But how often? As often as I think. For perhaps it could even happen, if I wholly ceased to think, that I would at the same time wholly cease to be. I now admit nothing that is not necessarily true. Precisely speaking, then, I am only a thinking thing, that is, a mind (mens sive animus), understanding, or reason, terms whose meaning I did not know before. Yet I am a real thing, and really exist. But what thing? I have answered: a thinking thing.

7. The question now arises: am I anything else besides? I will stir up my imagination to find out whether I am not something more than a thinking thing. Now it is plain that I am not the assemblage of limbs called the human body. I am not a thin and penetrating air spread through all these limbs, or wind, or flame, or vapor, or breath, or anything at all that I can imagine. For I supposed that all these did not exist, and, keeping that supposition, I still find that I am assured of my existence. But perhaps it is true that these very things which I suppose not to exist, because they are unknown to me, are in truth not different from the self that I do know. This I cannot decide, and I will not now argue about it. I can only judge of things that are known to me. I am conscious that I exist, and I, who know that I exist, ask what I am. It is perfectly certain, however, that my knowledge of my existence, taken in this precise sense, does not depend on things whose existence is not yet known to me. Consequently it does not depend on anything I can invent in imagination. Moreover, the very phrase I frame an image (effingo) reminds me of my error. For I would in truth be framing an image if I imagined myself to be anything, since to imagine is nothing but to contemplate the figure or image of a corporeal thing. But I already know that I exist, and that all these images, and in general everything relating to the nature of body, may be merely dreams [or chimeras]. From this I see that it is no more reasonable to say I will excite my imagination in order to know more distinctly what I am, than to say: I am now awake and perceive something real, but because my perception is not clear enough, I will go to sleep on purpose, so that my dreams may show me the object of my perception more truly and clearly. And therefore I know that nothing I can grasp in imagination belongs to the knowledge I have of myself, and that the mind must be called back with the utmost care from this way of thinking, so that it can know its own nature with perfect distinctness.

8. But what, then, am I? A thinking thing, it has been said. But what is a thinking thing? It is a thing that doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses, and that also imagines and perceives.

9. This is certainly not a small matter, if all these properties belong to my nature. But why should they not belong to it? Am I not that very being who now doubts almost everything, who nevertheless understands and conceives certain things, who affirms one alone to be true and denies the others, who desires to know more, and does not wish to be deceived, who imagines many things, sometimes even against his will, and who also perceives many things, as if through the senses? Is there anything in all this that is not as true as that I am, even if I were always dreaming, and even if he who gave me being used all his ingenuity to deceive me? Is there any one of these attributes that can properly be distinguished from my thought, or said to be separate from myself? For it is so evident of itself that it is I who doubt, I who understand, and I who desire, that nothing needs to be added to make it clearer. And I am certainly the same being who imagines. For although it may be (as I supposed before) that nothing I imagine is true, still the power of imagination does not cease really to exist in me and to form part of my thought. Finally, I am the same being who perceives, that is, who apprehends certain things as if by the organs of sense, since in truth I see light, hear a noise, and feel heat. But it will be said that these presentations are false and that I am dreaming. Let it be so. At all events it is certain that I seem to see light, hear a noise, and feel heat. This cannot be false, and this is what in me is properly called perceiving (sentire), which is nothing other than thinking.

10. From this I begin to know what I am a little more clearly and distinctly than before. But it still seems to me, and I cannot help believing, that corporeal things, whose images are formed by thought [which fall under the senses] and are examined by thought, are known much more distinctly than that part of myself, I know not what, which cannot be imagined. It may indeed seem strange to say that I know and comprehend more distinctly things whose existence appears doubtful to me, which are unknown and do not belong to me, than things of whose reality I am persuaded, which are known to me and belong to my own nature. In a word, it seems strange to say that I know them more distinctly than I know myself. But I see clearly what is happening. My mind likes to wander, and will not yet submit to being held within the limits of truth. Let us therefore leave the mind to itself once more, and give it every kind of liberty [to consider the objects that appear to it from outside], so that, having drawn it away from these gently and at the right moment [and fixed it on the consideration of its being and the properties it finds in itself], it may then be more easily controlled.

11. Let us now consider, then, the things commonly thought to be [the easiest to know, and also] the most distinctly known, namely the bodies we touch and see. I do not mean bodies in general, for these general notions are usually somewhat more confused, but one body in particular. Take, for example, this piece of wax. It is quite fresh, having only recently been taken from the beehive. It has not yet lost the sweetness of the honey it held. It still keeps something of the scent of the flowers it was gathered from. Its color, figure and size are apparent (to the sight). It is hard, cold and easy to handle, and it makes a sound when struck with the finger. In short, everything that helps make a body as distinctly known as possible is found in the one before us. But while I am speaking, let it be placed near the fire. What remained of the taste is released, the smell evaporates, the color changes, the figure is destroyed, the size increases, it becomes liquid, it grows hot, it can hardly be handled, and when struck it gives off no sound. Does the same wax still remain after this change? It must be admitted that it does remain. No one doubts it or judges otherwise. What was it, then, that I knew so distinctly in the piece of wax? Certainly it could be nothing of all that I observed by means of the senses, since everything that fell under taste, smell, sight, touch and hearing has changed, and yet the same wax remains.

12. Perhaps it was what I now think: that this wax was not the sweetness of honey, nor the pleasant scent of flowers, nor the whiteness, nor the figure, nor the sound, but only a body that a little earlier appeared to me under these forms and is now perceived under others. But to speak precisely, what is it that I imagine when I think of it in this way? Let us consider it attentively and, removing everything that does not belong to the wax, see what remains. Certainly nothing remains except something extended, flexible and movable. But what is meant by flexible and movable? Is it that I imagine that the piece of wax, being round, can become square, or pass from a square into a triangular figure? Certainly not, because I conceive that it admits of an infinity of such changes, and I cannot run through this infinity by imagination. Consequently, this conception I have of the wax is not produced by the faculty of imagination. But what now is this extension? Is it not also unknown? For it becomes greater when the wax is melted, greater when it is boiled, and greater still when the heat increases. And I would not conceive [clearly and] truly what the wax is if I did not suppose that the piece I am considering admits of an even wider variety of extension than I have ever imagined. I must therefore admit that I cannot even comprehend by imagination what this piece of wax is, and that it is the mind alone (mens, Lat., entendement, F.) which perceives it. I speak of one piece in particular, for as to wax in general this is still more evident. But what is this piece of wax that can be perceived only by the [understanding or] mind? It is certainly the same one that I see, touch and imagine; in short, it is the same one that I believed it to be from the beginning. But, and it is important to observe this, the perception of it is neither an act of sight, nor of touch, nor of imagination, and never was, though it formerly seemed so. It is simply an intuition (inspectio) of the mind. This intuition may be imperfect and confused, as it was before, or very clear and distinct, as it is now, depending on how much the attention is directed to the elements it contains and of which it is composed.

13. Meanwhile, I am greatly astonished when I observe [the weakness of my mind and] how prone it is to error. For although I consider all this silently in my own mind, without giving any expression to what I think, words still sometimes get in my way, and I am almost led into error by the terms of ordinary language. We say, for example, that we see the same wax when it is before us, and not that we judge it to be the same because it keeps the same color and figure. From this I would immediately be inclined to conclude that the wax is known by the act of sight and not by the intuition of the mind alone, were it not for a similar case: human beings passing in the street below, as seen from a window. In this case I do not hesitate to say that I see the men themselves, just as I say that I see the wax. Yet what do I see from the window besides hats and cloaks, which might cover artificial machines moved by springs? But from these appearances I judge that they are human beings. And so I comprehend, by the faculty of judgment alone which is in my mind, what I believed I saw with my eyes.

14. A man who aims to rise to knowledge above the common level ought to be ashamed to look for occasions of doubt in ordinary forms of speech. So, instead of doing this, I will proceed with the matter in hand and ask whether I perceived the piece of wax more clearly and perfectly when I first saw it, and thought I knew it by the external sense itself, or at least by the common sense (sensus communis), as it is called, that is, by the imaginative faculty, or whether I apprehend it more clearly now, after examining more carefully both what it is and how it can be known. It would certainly be ridiculous to doubt this. For what was distinct in that first perception? What did I perceive that any animal might not have perceived? But when I distinguish the wax from its external forms, and consider it quite naked, as if I had stripped off its clothes, it is certain that, although some error may still be found in my judgment, I cannot apprehend it in this way without having a human mind.

15. But finally, what shall I say of the mind itself, that is, of myself? For so far I admit that I am nothing but mind. What, then! I who seem to have so distinct an apprehension of the piece of wax, do I not know myself with greater truth and certainty, and also much more distinctly and clearly? For if I judge that the wax exists because I see it, it follows much more evidently, for the same reason, that I myself am or exist. For it is possible that what I see is not in truth wax, and that I do not even have eyes with which to see anything. But it cannot be that, when I see, or (which comes to the same thing) when I think I see, I who think am nothing. Likewise, if I judge that the wax exists because I touch it, it will again follow that I am. And if I determine that my imagination, or any other cause whatever, persuades me of the existence of the wax, I will draw the same conclusion again. And what is remarked here of the piece of wax applies to all the other things that are external to me. Further, if the [notion or] perception of wax seemed to me more precise and distinct once not only sight and touch but many other causes besides had made it manifest to my apprehension, how much more distinctly must I now know myself, since all the reasons that contribute to knowing the nature of wax, or of any body whatever, show the nature of my mind even better! And there are so many other things in the mind itself that help to illustrate its nature that those depending on the body, to which I have referred here, hardly deserve to be taken into account.

16. But, in conclusion, I find I have returned without noticing to the point I wanted. For it is now manifest to me that bodies themselves are properly perceived not by the senses or the faculty of imagination but by the intellect alone, and that they are perceived not because they are seen and touched but only because they are understood [or rightly comprehended by thought]. So I readily discover that nothing is more easily or clearly apprehended than my own mind. But it is difficult to rid oneself so quickly of an opinion one has long been used to. So it will be desirable to stay for some time at this stage, so that by long continued meditation I may impress this new knowledge more deeply on my memory.

chapters.title: Meditation 3 — Of God: That He Exists
paragraphs: 1. I will now close my eyes, stop my ears and turn my senses away from their objects. I will even wipe from my consciousness all the images of corporeal things; or, since that can hardly be done, I will at least regard them as empty and false. Holding conversation only with myself and examining my nature closely, I will try to gain, step by step, a more intimate and familiar knowledge of myself. I am a thinking (conscious) thing, that is, a being who doubts, affirms, denies, knows a few things and is ignorant of many — [who loves, hates], wills, refuses, and who also imagines and perceives. For, as I remarked before, the things I perceive or imagine are perhaps nothing at all apart from me [and in themselves]; yet I am assured that those modes of consciousness I call perceptions and imaginations exist in me, but only insofar as they are modes of consciousness.

2. In the little I have said, I think I have summed up everything I really know, or at least everything I was aware, up to now, that I knew. Since I am trying to extend my knowledge further, I will proceed with care and consider whether I can still find in myself anything more that I have not yet noticed. I am certain that I am a thinking thing. Do I not then also know what is required to make me certain of a truth? In this first knowledge there is doubtless nothing that assures me of its truth except the clear and distinct perception of what I affirm. That would not be enough to assure me that what I say is true, if it could ever happen that something I perceived so clearly and distinctly turned out to be false. Accordingly, it seems to me that I may now take as a general rule that everything very clearly and distinctly apprehended (conceived) is true.

3. Nevertheless, I once accepted many things as wholly certain and manifest which I later found to be doubtful. What were they? The earth, the sky, the stars, and all the other objects I used to perceive by the senses. But what did I clearly [and distinctly] perceive in them? Only that the ideas and thoughts of those objects were present to my mind. Even now I do not deny that these ideas are in my mind. But I affirmed one more thing, which I thought I clearly perceived because I was used to believing it, although in truth I did not perceive it at all: namely, that there exist objects outside me from which those ideas proceed and which they perfectly resemble. Here I was mistaken; or if I judged correctly, this was certainly not owing to any knowledge I possessed (the force of my perception, Lat.).

4. But when I considered something in arithmetic or geometry that was very simple and easy, such as that two and three added together make five, did I not see it at least clearly enough to affirm that it is true? Indeed, if I later judged that we ought to doubt such things, it was only because it occurred to me that God might perhaps have given me a nature such that I would be deceived even about the matters that seemed to me most evidently true. Yet whenever this preconceived opinion about the sovereign power of a God comes to mind, I am forced to admit that it is easy for him, if he wishes, to make me err even where I think I have the highest evidence. On the other hand, whenever I turn my attention to things I think I apprehend with great clearness, I am so persuaded of their truth that I spontaneously say: Deceive me who may, no one will ever be able to bring it about that I am not, as long as I am conscious that I am; nor, at any future time, make it true that I have never been, since it is now true that I am; nor make two and three more or less than five. In supposing these and other such absurdities, I discover a manifest contradiction. And in truth, since I have no ground for believing that Deity is deceitful, and have not even considered the reasons that establish the existence of a Deity of any kind, the ground of doubt resting only on this supposition is very slight, and, so to speak, metaphysical. But in order to remove it entirely, I must inquire whether there is a God as soon as I have the opportunity; and if I find that there is, I must also examine whether he can be a deceiver. For without knowing these two truths, I do not see that I can ever be certain of anything. To examine this without breaking the order of meditation I have set myself [which is to pass by degrees from the notions I find first in my mind to those I shall afterward discover in it], it is necessary at this stage to divide all my thoughts into certain classes, and to consider in which of these classes truth and error are, strictly speaking, to be found.

5. Some of my thoughts are, as it were, images of things, and to these alone the name IDEA properly belongs, as when I think [represent to my mind] a man, a chimera, the sky, an angel or God. Others take other forms. When I will, fear, affirm or deny, I always apprehend something as the object of my thought, but I also embrace in thought something more than the representation of that object. Of this class of thoughts, some are called volitions or affections, and others judgments.

6. Now ideas, if considered only in themselves and not referred to anything beyond them, cannot, properly speaking, be false. Whether I imagine a goat or a chimera, it is equally true that I imagine the one and the other. Nor need we fear that falsity may lie in the will or the affections: I may desire wrong things, even things that never existed, but it is still true that I desire them. So only our judgments remain, and in them we must take diligent care not to be deceived. The chief and most common error in them is to judge that the ideas in us are like, or conform to, things outside us. Certainly, if we considered the ideas themselves only as modes of our thought (consciousness), without referring them to anything beyond, they would hardly give any occasion for error.

7. Among these ideas, some seem to me innate, others adventitious, and others made by myself (factitious). For I have the power of conceiving what is called a thing, or a truth, or a thought, and it seems to me that I hold this power from no source other than my own nature. But when I hear a noise, see the sun or feel heat, I have always judged that these sensations came from certain objects existing outside me. And, in short, sirens, hippogryphs and the like appear to me to be inventions of my own mind. Yet I may perhaps even come to think that all my ideas are of the class I call adventitious, or that they are all innate, or that they are all factitious; for I have not yet clearly discovered their true origin.

8. My main task here is to consider, regarding the ideas that appear to come from certain objects outside me, what grounds there are for thinking them like those objects. The first ground is that nature seems to teach me so. The second is that I am conscious that these ideas do not depend on my will, and therefore not on myself; for they are often presented to me against my will. At present, for instance, whether I will or not, I feel heat; and so I am persuaded that this sensation or idea (sensum vel ideam) of heat is produced in me by something different from myself, namely, the heat of the fire by which I sit. And it is very reasonable to suppose that this object impresses on me its own likeness rather than anything else.

9. But I must consider whether these reasons are strong and convincing enough. When I speak of being taught by nature here, I understand by the word nature only a certain spontaneous impulse that leads me to believe in a resemblance between ideas and their objects. I do not mean a natural light that gives knowledge of its truth. These two things are widely different. What the natural light shows to be true cannot be in any degree doubtful, as, for example, that I am because I doubt, and other truths of that kind; for I possess no other faculty by which to distinguish truth from error that could teach me that what the natural light declares true is false and that is equally trustworthy. But as for [seemingly] natural impulses, I have observed, when the question was the choice of right or wrong in action, that they often led me to take the worse side. And I do not see that I have any better ground for following them in matters of truth and error.

10. Then, as to the other reason, that these ideas must arise from objects outside me because they do not depend on my will, I do not find it more convincing than the first. Just as the natural impulses I have just spoken of are found in me even though they are not always in harmony with my will, so it may be that I have some power, not sufficiently known to myself, capable of producing ideas without the help of external objects. Indeed, it has always seemed to me that ideas are formed in this way during sleep, by some such power, with nothing external to help.

11. And finally, even if I granted that they proceeded from those objects, it does not necessarily follow that they must be like them. On the contrary, I have observed in many cases a great difference between the object and its idea. For example, I find in my mind two wholly different ideas of the sun. One, by which it appears extremely small, derives from the senses and should be placed among adventitious ideas. The other, by which it seems many times larger than the whole earth, is adopted on astronomical grounds, that is, drawn out of certain notions born with me, or else framed by myself in some other way. These two ideas certainly cannot both resemble the same sun; and reason teaches me that the one which seems to have come most directly from it is the most unlike.

12. These things sufficiently prove that, up to now, it has not been by a certain and deliberate judgment but only by a sort of blind impulse that I have believed in the existence of certain things different from myself, which, through the organs of sense or by whatever other means, conveyed their ideas or images into my mind [and impressed it with their likenesses].

13. But there is another way of inquiring whether any of the objects whose ideas are in my mind exist outside me. If ideas are taken only insofar as they are modes of consciousness, I notice no difference or inequality among them, and all seem to proceed from myself in the same manner. But if I consider them as images, one representing one thing and another a different thing, it is evident that there is great diversity among them. Without doubt, those that represent substances are something more, and contain in themselves, so to speak, more objective reality [that is, participate by representation in higher degrees of being or perfection], than those that represent only modes or accidents. Again, the idea by which I conceive a God [sovereign], eternal, infinite, [immutable], all-knowing, all-powerful and creator of all things outside himself — this idea, I say, certainly has in it more objective reality than the ideas that represent finite substances.

14. Now it is manifest by the natural light that there must be at least as much reality in the efficient and total cause as in its effect. For where could the effect draw its reality if not from its cause? And how could the cause give it this reality unless it had it in itself? Hence it follows not only that what is cannot be produced by what is not, but also that the more perfect, that is, what contains in itself more reality, cannot be the effect of the less perfect. This is evidently true not only of effects whose reality is actual or formal, but also of ideas, whose reality is considered only as objective. For example, a stone that does not yet exist cannot begin to be unless it is produced by something that has in itself, formally or eminently, everything that enters into its composition [in other words, by something that contains in itself the same properties as the stone, or higher ones]. Likewise, heat can be produced in a subject that was previously without it only by a cause of an order [degree or kind] at least as perfect as heat; and so with the rest. Further, even the idea of heat, or of the stone, cannot exist in me unless some cause puts it there, a cause that contains at least as much reality as I conceive to be in the heat or the stone. For although that cause may pass nothing of its actual or formal reality into my idea, we ought not on that account to imagine that it is less real. We ought to consider that, [since every idea is a work of the mind], its nature is such that it requires no formal reality other than what it borrows from my consciousness, of which it is only a mode [that is, a manner or way of thinking]. But for an idea to contain this objective reality rather than that, it must doubtless derive it from some cause in which there is at least as much formal reality as the idea contains of objective reality; for if we suppose that an idea contains anything that was not in its cause, it must of course derive this from nothing. However imperfect the mode of existence by which a thing is objectively [or by representation] in the understanding through its idea, we certainly cannot, for all that, say that this mode of existence is nothing, nor, consequently, that the idea owes its origin to nothing.

15. Nor should we imagine that, because the reality I consider in these ideas is only objective, the same reality need not be present formally (actually) in their causes, but only objectively. For just as the objective mode of existing belongs to ideas by their own nature, so the formal mode of existing belongs by its own nature to the causes of these ideas (at least to the first and principal ones). And although one idea may give rise to another, this regress cannot go on infinitely; we must in the end reach a first idea, whose cause is, as it were, the archetype, containing formally [and in act] all the reality [or perfection] found objectively [or by representation] in these ideas. So I am clearly taught by the natural light that ideas exist in me as pictures or images. These may readily fall short of the perfection of the objects they are taken from, but can never contain anything greater or more perfect.

16. The longer and more carefully I examine all these matters, the more the conviction of their truth brightens and becomes distinct. But to sum up, what conclusion shall I draw from it all? It is this. If the objective reality [or perfection] of any one of my ideas is such as to convince me clearly that this same reality exists in me neither formally nor eminently, and if it follows that I myself cannot be the cause of it, then it is a necessary consequence that I am not alone in the world, but that some other being besides myself exists as the cause of that idea. If, on the contrary, no such idea is found in my mind, I shall have no sufficient ground of assurance of the existence of any being besides myself; for after the most careful search, I have so far been unable to find any other ground.

17. Now among my ideas, besides the one that represents myself, about which there can be no difficulty here, there is one that represents a God; others that represent corporeal and inanimate things; others, angels; others, animals; and finally some that represent men like myself.

18. As for the ideas that represent other men, animals or angels, I can easily suppose that they were formed by mixing and combining the other ideas I have, of myself, of corporeal things and of God, even if there were, apart from me, no men, animals or angels.

19. As for the ideas of corporeal objects, I never found in them anything so great or excellent that I did not seem capable of originating it myself. For when I examine these ideas closely and one by one, as I examined the idea of wax yesterday, I find that little in them is clearly and distinctly perceived. In the class of things clearly apprehended I recognize the following, namely: magnitude or extension in length, breadth and depth; figure, which results from the limiting of extension; situation, which bodies of different figures keep in relation to one another; and motion, or change of situation; to which may be added substance, duration and number. But light, colors, sounds, odors, tastes, heat, cold and the other tactile qualities are thought with so much obscurity and confusion that I cannot even determine whether they are true or false; in other words, whether or not the ideas I have of these qualities are in truth ideas of real objects. For although I remarked before that formal falsity, or falsity properly so called, can be found only in judgments, there may nevertheless be found in ideas a certain material falsity, which arises when they represent what is nothing as if it were something. For example, my ideas of cold and heat are so far from clear and distinct that I cannot tell from them whether cold is only the privation of heat, or heat the privation of cold; or whether they are or are not real qualities. And since, ideas being as it were images, there can be none that does not seem to us to represent some object, the idea that represents cold as something real and positive will not improperly be called false, if it is correct to say that cold is nothing but a privation of heat; and so in other cases.

20. For ideas of this kind I need not assign any author besides myself. If they are false, that is, represent unreal objects, the natural light teaches me that they proceed from nothing; in other words, that they are in me only because something is lacking to the perfection of my nature. But if they are true, then, since they show me so little reality that I cannot even distinguish the object represented from nonbeing, I do not see why I should not be their author.

21. Among the clear and distinct ideas of corporeal things, there are some which, as it appears to me, might have been taken from the idea I have of myself: those of substance, duration, number and the like. When I think that a stone is a substance, or a thing capable of existing of itself, and that I am also a substance, I conceive that I am a thinking and non-extended thing and that the stone, on the contrary, is extended and unconscious, so that there is the greatest diversity between the two concepts; yet these two ideas seem to have this in common, that they both represent substances. In the same way, when I think of myself as existing now, recall that I existed some time ago, and am conscious of various thoughts whose number I know, I acquire the ideas of duration and number, which I can afterward transfer to as many objects as I please. As for the other qualities that make up the ideas of corporeal objects, namely extension, figure, situation and motion, it is true that they are not in me formally, since I am merely a thinking being. But because they are only certain modes of substance, and I myself am a substance, it seems possible that they may be contained in me eminently.

22. There remains, therefore, only the idea of God, in which I must consider whether there is anything that cannot be supposed to originate with myself. By the name God I understand a substance that is infinite, [eternal, immutable], independent, all-knowing, all-powerful, and by which I myself and everything else that exists, if anything else does, were created. These properties are so great and excellent that the more attentively I consider them, the less I am persuaded that my idea of them owes its origin to myself alone. And so it is absolutely necessary to conclude, from all I have said before, that God exists.

23. For although the idea of substance is in my mind because I myself am a substance, I would not have the idea of an infinite substance, since I am a finite being, unless it were given to me by some substance that is in reality infinite.

24. And I must not imagine that I apprehend the infinite not by a true idea but only by the negation of the finite, as I comprehend rest and darkness by the negation of motion and light. On the contrary, I clearly perceive that there is more reality in infinite substance than in finite, and therefore that I have in some way the perception (notion) of the infinite before that of the finite, that is, the perception of God before that of myself. For how could I know that I doubt, that I desire, that something is wanting to me and that I am not wholly perfect, if I had no idea of a being more perfect than myself, by comparison with which I recognized the deficiencies of my nature?

25. And it cannot be said that this idea of God is perhaps materially false, and consequently that it may have arisen from nothing [in other words, that it may exist in me because of my imperfections, as I said before of the ideas of heat and cold and the like: for, on the contrary, since this idea is very clear and distinct and contains in itself more objective reality than any other, no idea is in itself more true or less open to the suspicion of falsity. The idea, I say, of a being supremely perfect and infinite is in the highest degree true; for although, perhaps, we may imagine that such a being does not exist, we cannot suppose that his idea represents nothing real, as I have already said of the idea of cold. It is likewise clear and distinct in the highest degree, since whatever the mind clearly and distinctly conceives as real or true, and as implying any perfection, is contained entire in this idea. This remains true even though I do not comprehend the infinite, and even though there may be in God an infinity of things that I cannot comprehend, or perhaps even reach by thought in any way. For it is of the nature of the infinite that it is not comprehended by the finite. It is enough that I rightly understand this, and judge that everything I clearly perceive, and in which I know there is some perfection, and perhaps also an infinity of properties of which I am ignorant, is formally or eminently in God; so that the idea I have of him becomes the most true, clear and distinct of all the ideas in my mind.

26. But perhaps I am something more than I suppose myself to be, and perhaps all the perfections I attribute to God exist in me in some way potentially, although they do not yet show themselves and have not been brought into act. Indeed, I am already conscious that my knowledge is increasing [and being perfected] by degrees; and I see nothing to prevent it from increasing thus to infinity, nor any reason why, once it has so increased and been perfected, I should not be able to acquire by it all the other perfections of the Divine nature. Nor, in short, do I see why the power I have of acquiring those perfections, if it really exists in me now, should not be sufficient to produce the ideas of them.

27. Yet on looking more closely into the matter I discover that this cannot be. In the first place, even if it were true that my knowledge daily acquired new degrees of perfection, and that there were potentially in my nature much that was not yet actually in it, still none of these excellences comes the slightest way near the idea I have of the Deity, in whom there is no perfection merely potentially [but all actually] existent. For it is an unmistakable token of imperfection in my knowledge that it is increased by degrees. Further, although my knowledge may increase more and more, I am not therefore led to think that it will ever be actually infinite, since it can never reach a point beyond which it is incapable of further increase. But I conceive God as actually infinite, so that nothing can be added to his perfection. And finally, I readily perceive that the objective being of an idea cannot be produced by a being that is merely potentially existent, which, properly speaking, is nothing, but only by a being existing formally or actually.

28. And truly, I see nothing in all I have just said that is not easy for anyone who considers it carefully to discern by the natural light. But when I let my attention relax somewhat, the vision of my mind is obscured and, as it were, blinded by the images of sensible objects, and I do not readily remember why the idea of a being more perfect than myself must of necessity have proceeded from a being that is in reality more perfect. For this reason I want to inquire further whether I, who have this idea of God, could exist if there were no God.

29. And I ask, from whom could I, in that case, derive my existence? Perhaps from myself, or from my parents, or from some other causes less perfect than God; for nothing more perfect than God, or even equal to him, can be thought or imagined.

30. Suppose I [were independent of every other existence, and] were the author of my own being. I would then doubt nothing and desire nothing, and I would lack no perfection at all, since I would have given myself every perfection whose idea I possess; in that case I would be God. Nor should anyone imagine that what I now lack might be harder to obtain than what I already have. Quite the opposite is manifest: it was far harder for me, a thinking being, to come out of nothing than it would be to gain knowledge of the many things I do not know, which are only the accidents of a thinking substance. Certainly, if I had of myself the greater perfection just mentioned [in other words, if I were the author of my own existence], I would at least not have refused myself the things that are easier to get [such as that infinite variety of knowledge I presently lack]. In fact I could not have refused myself any property I perceive in the idea of God, because none of them seems harder to make or acquire than the rest. And if one of them did turn out harder, it would certainly look that way to me (supposing I were the source of everything else I have), since I would find in it a limit to my power.

31. Nor would it help to suppose that I have always been as I am now: that would not let me escape these reasonings, because even then it would not follow that I need not look for an author of my existence. For the whole span of my life divides into infinitely many parts, and none of them depends on any other. So the fact that I existed a little while ago does not mean I must exist now, unless some cause creates me afresh at this moment, so to speak, that is, conserves me. Anyone who attentively considers the nature of duration will see perfectly clearly that a substance needs the same power and the same act to be conserved at each moment of its duration as it would need to be created if it did not yet exist. It is therefore manifestly a dictate of the natural light that conservation and creation differ only in our mode of thinking [and not in reality].

32. What is needed here, therefore, is only to ask myself whether I have some power by which I can make myself, who exist now, still exist a moment from now.
