For since I am merely a thinking thing (or at least, since the question for the moment concerns only that part of me), I would undoubtedly be conscious of such a power if it were in me. But I am conscious of none; and from this I manifestly know that I depend on some being other than myself.

33. Perhaps, though, the being I depend on is not God, and my parents or some causes less perfect than Deity produced me. That cannot be. As I said earlier, it is perfectly evident that there must be at least as much reality in the cause as in its effect. And so, since I am a thinking thing with an idea of God in me, whatever the cause of my existence ultimately is, it must necessarily be admitted to be a thinking being too, one that has in itself the idea and all the perfections I attribute to Deity. One may then ask again whether this cause derives its origin and existence from itself or from another cause. If it is self-existent, then by what I have already laid down, this cause is God: having the perfection of self-existence, it must also, without doubt, be able to possess in actuality every perfection whose idea it has — in other words, all the perfections I conceive to belong to God. If instead it owes its existence to a cause other than itself, we ask again, for the same reason, whether this second cause exists of itself or through another, until, stage by stage, we reach a final cause, and that will be God.

34. It is quite manifest, too, that there can be no infinite regress of causes here, because the question is not so much about the cause that once produced me as about the cause that conserves me at this very moment.

35. Nor can we suppose that several causes together produced me, so that I got the idea of one perfection I attribute to Deity from one cause and the idea of another from another, and that all those perfections are found somewhere in the universe but not all together in a single being, God. The reverse is the case: the unity, simplicity and inseparability of all the properties of Deity is itself one of the chief perfections I conceive him to have. The idea of this unity of all the perfections of Deity could certainly not have been put in my mind by a cause from which I had not also received the ideas of all the other perfections. For no power could make me grasp them in one inseparable unity without also giving me knowledge of what they were [and of their existence in a particular mode].

36. Finally, take my parents [from whom it appears I sprang]. Even if all I have believed about them is true, it still does not follow that they conserve me, or even that they produced me, in so far as I am a thinking being. The most they did toward my origin was to give certain dispositions (modifications) to the matter in which I have until now judged that I am enclosed — I, or my mind, which is all that I now take myself to be. So they raise no difficulty here, and from this alone — that I exist and have the idea of a being absolutely perfect, that is, of God — it must necessarily be concluded that his existence is most clearly demonstrated.

37. It remains only to ask how I received this idea from God, for I did not draw it from the senses, and it does not come upon me unexpectedly, as ideas of sensible objects usually do when these objects are presented, or seem to be presented, to the external sense organs. Nor is it merely something my mind made up or invented, since I cannot take anything away from it or add anything to it. The only alternative left, then, is that it is innate, as the idea of myself is.

38. And it is no wonder that God, when he created me, implanted this idea in me, to be like the mark a workman leaves on his work. The mark need not be anything distinct from the work itself. Considering only that God is my creator, it is highly probable that he made me in some way after his own image and likeness, and that I perceive this likeness, which includes the idea of God, with the same faculty by which I apprehend myself. That is to say, when I reflect on myself, I find not only that I am an incomplete, [imperfect] and dependent being, who constantly aspires to something better and greater than he is. I am also assured that the being I depend on has in himself all the goods I aspire to [and the ideas of which I find in my mind], having them not just indefinitely and potentially but infinitely and actually, and that he is therefore God. The whole force of the argument I have used to establish God's existence is this: I perceive that I could not possibly have the nature I have, and also have in my mind the idea of a God, unless God really existed — the very God, I say, whose idea is in my mind, that is, a being with all those lofty perfections which the mind can conceive only slightly, without being able fully to comprehend them, and who is wholly above all defect [and has nothing that marks imperfection]. It is sufficiently manifest from this that he cannot be a deceiver, since it is a dictate of the natural light that all fraud and deception come from some defect.

39. Before I examine this more attentively and move on to other truths that can be drawn from it, I think it right to stay here for a while and contemplate God himself — to ponder his marvelous attributes at leisure, and to behold, admire and adore the beauty of this light so unspeakably great, as far, at least, as the strength of my mind, somewhat dazzled by the sight, will permit. For just as we learn by faith that the supreme felicity of the next life lies in contemplating the Divine majesty alone, so we learn from experience even now that a similar meditation, though incomparably less perfect, gives the highest satisfaction we are capable of in this life.

chapters.title: Meditation 4 — Of Truth and Error
paragraphs: 1. For some days now I have been training myself to detach my mind from the senses. I have carefully noticed that very little is known with certainty about corporeal objects, that we know much more about the human mind, and still more about God himself. As a result I can now easily turn my mind away from [sensible or] imaginable objects and direct it to those that are free of all matter and purely intelligible. The idea I have of the human mind, as a thinking thing that is not extended in length, breadth and depth and shares none of the properties of body, is certainly incomparably more distinct than my idea of any corporeal object. And when I consider that I doubt, in other words that I am an incomplete and dependent being, the idea of a complete and independent being, that is, of God, presents itself to my mind with such clearness and distinctness. From the mere fact that this idea is in me, or that I who have it exist, it follows so manifestly that God exists, and that my own existence at every moment depends entirely on him, that I am led to believe the human mind can know nothing with greater clearness and certitude. And now I seem to see a path leading from the contemplation of the true God, in whom are contained all the treasures of science and wisdom, to the knowledge of the other things in the universe.

2. For, first, I discover that it is impossible for him ever to deceive me, since every kind of fraud and deceit involves some imperfection. The ability to deceive may seem a sign of subtlety or power, but the will to deceive undoubtedly testifies to malice and weakness, and these cannot be found in God.

3. Second, I am conscious of having a certain faculty of judging [or discerning truth from error]. I doubtless received it from God, together with everything else I have. Since he cannot will to deceive me, it is likewise certain that he has not given me a faculty that would ever lead me into error, provided I use it rightly.

4. There would be no doubt left on this point, except that it seems to imply that I can never be deceived. For if everything I have comes from God, and he put no deceitful faculty in me, it seems to follow that I can never fall into error. And it is true that when I think only of God (when I look upon myself as coming from God, Fr.) and turn wholly to him, I find [in myself] no cause of error or falsity. But as soon as I turn back to myself, experience assures me that I am nevertheless subject to countless errors. When I look for the cause of these, I notice that my consciousness holds not only a real and positive idea of God, that is, of a being supremely perfect, but also, so to speak, a certain negative idea of nothing, in other words of what is infinitely distant from every sort of perfection. I notice that I am, as it were, something intermediate between God and nothing, standing between absolute existence and non-existence. Thus, in so far as an absolute being is my creator, there is truly nothing in me that could lead me into error; but, in so far as I also share in some degree in nothing or nonbeing, that is, am not myself the supreme Being and lack many perfections, it is not surprising that I fall into error. From this I see that error, as far as it is error, is not something real that depends on God for its existence; it is simply defect. So God did not need to give me a faculty expressly for falling into error. I am deceived because the power God has given me to discern truth from error is not infinite.

5. Still, this does not yet fully satisfy me. For error is not a pure negation, [in other words, not just the lack of some knowledge that is not owed to me]; it is a privation, the lack of some knowledge that it seems I ought to have. Yet when I think about the nature of God, it seems impossible that he would have planted in his creature a faculty not perfect of its kind, that is, one lacking a perfection that is due to it; for if it is true that the more skillful the maker, the more perfect his work, what could the supreme Creator of the universe have made that is not absolutely perfect in all its parts? And surely there is no doubt that God could have created me so that I would never be deceived; it is also certain that he always wills what is best. Is it better, then, for me to be capable of being deceived than not to be?

6. When I reflect on this more attentively, the first thing that strikes me is that I should not be surprised if I cannot always grasp why God acts as he does. Nor should I doubt that he exists just because I find, perhaps, that there are various other things besides this one whose why and how I do not understand. For I already know that my nature is extremely weak and limited and that God's nature, by contrast, is immense, incomprehensible and infinite. So I no longer find it hard to see that he has in his power an infinity of things whose causes are beyond my mind's grasp. This consideration alone is enough to convince me that the whole class of final causes is of no use in physical [or natural] things; for I think I cannot, without exposing myself to the charge of temerity, try to discover the [impenetrable] ends of Deity.

7. It also strikes me that, to judge the perfection of the works of Deity, we should not look at one creature in isolation but at all his creatures together. For something that might perhaps, with some show of reason, seem highly imperfect if it were alone in the world may still be the most perfect possible when seen as a part of the whole universe. It was my purpose to doubt everything, and so far I know with certainty only my own existence and God's. Nevertheless, having noted the infinite power of Deity, I cannot deny that he may have produced many other objects, or at least that he is able to produce them, so that I may have a place as a part in relation to the great whole of his creatures.

8. Now I look at myself more closely and ask what my errors are (which alone show that there is imperfection in me). I observe that they depend on two causes working together: the faculty of cognition I have, and the faculty of election or power of free choice — in other words, the understanding and the will. For by the understanding alone I [neither affirm nor deny anything but] merely apprehend (percipio) the ideas about which I can form a judgment, and when it is taken precisely in this way, no error properly so called is found in it. There are perhaps countless objects in the world of which I have no idea in my understanding. Still, it cannot be said that I am deprived of those ideas [as of something due to my nature]; I simply do not have them. For there is really no ground for proving that Deity ought to have given me a larger faculty of cognition than he did. However skillful a workman I take him to be, I have no reason to think he was bound to give each of his works all the perfections he can give to some. Nor can I complain that God has not given me freedom of choice, or a will ample and perfect enough, since I am conscious of a will so wide and extended that it is superior to all limits. What strikes me as highly remarkable here is that among all my other properties there is none so great and perfect that I do not clearly discern it could be greater and more perfect still. Take the faculty of understanding: I find it very small in extent and greatly limited, and yet I form the idea of another faculty of the same nature, much more ample and even infinite; and since I can frame the idea of it, I discover from that fact alone that it belongs to the nature of God. Likewise, if I examine memory or imagination or any other faculty I have, I find each one small and circumscribed, and in God immense [and infinite]. It is only the faculty of will, or freedom of choice, that I experience to be so great that I cannot conceive the idea of one more ample and extended. So it is chiefly my will that makes me discern that I bear a certain image and similitude of Deity. For although the faculty of will is incomparably greater in God than in me, both because of the knowledge and power joined with it, which make it stronger and more efficacious, and because of its object, since in him it extends to more things, it nevertheless does not appear to me greater, considered in itself formally and precisely. For the power of will consists only in this: that we are able to do or not to do the same thing (that is, to affirm or deny, to pursue or shun it); or, better, in this alone: that when we affirm or deny, pursue or shun, what the understanding proposes to us, we act without being conscious of any external force determining us to a particular action. For freedom does not require me to be equally indifferent toward each of two contraries. On the contrary, the more I incline toward one of them, whether because I clearly know that the reason of truth and goodness is in it or because God so disposes my thought from within, the more freely I choose and embrace it. Divine grace and natural knowledge, far from reducing liberty, assuredly increase and strengthen it. The indifference I am conscious of when no reason impels me to one side rather than the other is the lowest grade of liberty: it shows a defect or negation of knowledge rather than a perfection of will. For if I always clearly knew what was true and good, I would never have trouble deciding what judgment to form or what choice to make, and so I would be entirely free without ever being indifferent.

9. From all this I discover, however, that the source of my errors is neither the power of willing I received from God, which is in its kind exceedingly ample and perfect, nor the power of understanding. For I conceive nothing except by the faculty God gave me, so whatever I conceive is doubtless rightly conceived, and I cannot be deceived in it. Where, then, do my errors come from? Only from this: I do not hold the will, whose range is much wider than that of the understanding, within the same limits, but extend it even to things I do not understand. The will is of itself indifferent to such things, and so it readily falls into error and sin, choosing the false in place of the true and evil in place of good.

10. Take an example. Not long ago I asked whether anything really existed in the world, and I found that, from the very fact of asking this question, it followed very manifestly that I myself existed. I could not help judging that what I conceived so clearly was true. No external cause forced this judgment on me; great clearness in the understanding was simply followed by a strong inclination in the will, and I believed it the more freely and spontaneously the less indifferent I was about it. Now, however, I know not only that I exist, in so far as I am a thinking being, but there is also presented to my mind a certain idea of corporeal nature. So I am in doubt whether the thinking nature that is in me, or rather that I myself am, differs from that corporeal nature, or whether the two are merely one and the same. I suppose here that I do not yet know of any reason to decide me for one belief over the other. It follows that it is a matter of perfect indifference to me which of the two suppositions I affirm or deny, or whether I form any judgment on the matter at all.

11. This indifference, moreover, covers not only things the understanding knows nothing about, but in general everything it does not discover with perfect clearness at the moment the will is deliberating about it. For however probable the conjectures that incline me to a judgment on some matter, merely knowing that they are conjectures, and not certain and indubitable reasons, is enough to lead me to the directly opposite judgment. I recently had ample experience of this, when I set aside as false everything I had previously held true, on the single ground that I could in some degree doubt it.

12. If I refrain from judging a thing when I do not conceive it with sufficient clearness and distinctness, it is plain that I act rightly and am not deceived. But if I resolve to deny or affirm, then I do not use my free will rightly; and if I affirm what is false, it is evident that I am deceived. Even if I judge in accordance with truth, I hit on it by chance, and I still do not escape the charge of misusing my freedom; for it is a dictate of the natural light that the knowledge of the understanding should always come before the determination of the will. In this misuse of the freedom of the will lies the privation that makes up the form of error. The privation, I say, is found in the act in so far as it comes from me; it is not in the faculty I received from God, nor even in the act in so far as it depends on him.

13. For I certainly have no reason to complain that God has not given me a greater power of intelligence or a more perfect natural light than he has, since it is in the nature of a finite understanding not to comprehend many things, and in the nature of a created understanding to be finite. Rather, I have every reason to thank God, who owed me nothing, for giving me all the perfections I have, and I should be far from thinking he has unjustly deprived me of the other perfections or kept them back from me.

14. Nor do I have reason to complain that he gave me a will more ample than my understanding. Since the will consists of a single indivisible element, it seems that nothing could be taken from it [without destroying it]. And certainly the more extensive it is, the more reason I have to thank the goodness of the one who gave it to me.

15. And finally, I should not complain that God concurs with me in forming the acts of this will, the judgments in which I am deceived, because, in so far as they depend on God, those acts are wholly true and good, and being able to form them is a higher degree of perfection in my nature than being unable would be. Privation, in which alone the formal reason of error and sin consists, needs no concurrence of Deity, because it is not a thing [or existence]; and if it is referred to God as its cause, it should be called not privation but negation [in the sense these words have in the schools]. For in truth it is no imperfection in Deity that he has given me the power to give or withhold my assent on certain matters of which he has not put a clear and distinct knowledge in my understanding. But it is doubtless an imperfection in me that I do not use my freedom rightly, and readily pass judgment on matters I conceive only obscurely and confusedly. I perceive, nevertheless, that Deity could easily have made me so that I would never be deceived while still remaining free and having limited knowledge. He could have done this by implanting in my understanding a clear and distinct knowledge of everything I would ever have to deliberate about; or simply by engraving so deeply on my memory the resolution never to judge anything without first conceiving it clearly and distinctly that I could never forget it. And I easily understand that, considering myself as a single whole, with no reference to any other being in the universe, I would have been much more perfect than I am if Deity had created me superior to error. But I cannot therefore deny that it is somehow a greater perfection in the universe for some of its parts not to be exempt from defect, as others are, than for all of them to be perfectly alike. And I have no right to complain that God, who placed me in the world, did not want me to hold that rank which is the chief and most perfect of all.

16. I even have good reason to be content, because if he has not given me the perfection of being superior to error by the first means I noted above, which depends on clear and evident knowledge of everything I can deliberate about, he has at least left in my power the other means: to hold firmly to the resolution never to judge where the truth is not clearly known to me. For, although I am conscious of the weakness that I cannot keep my mind continually fixed on the same thought, I can nevertheless, by attentive and oft-repeated meditation, impress that resolution so strongly on my memory that I will never fail to recall it when I need it, and in this way I can acquire the habit of not erring.

17. Since the highest and chief perfection of man consists in being superior to error, I judge that I have gained no small thing from this day's meditation, because I have discovered the source of error and falsity. It can certainly be nothing other than what I have just explained. For whenever I restrain my will within the limits of my knowledge, so that it forms a judgment only about objects clearly and distinctly represented to it by the understanding, I can never be deceived; because every clear and distinct conception is doubtless something, and as such cannot owe its origin to nothing, but must necessarily have God as its author — God, I say, who, being supremely perfect, cannot without contradiction be the cause of any error. Consequently it must be concluded that every such conception [or judgment] is true. And today I have learned not only what I must avoid in order to escape error but also what I must do to arrive at the knowledge of truth. For I will assuredly reach truth if I give sufficient attention to everything I conceive perfectly, and separate it from the things I conceive more confusedly and obscurely; and to this I shall give diligent heed from now on.

chapters.title: Meditation 5 — Of the Essence of Material Things; And, Again, Of God: That He Exists
paragraphs: 1. Several other questions remain about the attributes of God and about my own nature, that is, my mind. Perhaps I will take up the investigation of these some other time. For now, I have found out what to do and what to avoid in order to reach the knowledge of truth. So my main task is to try to climb out of the state of doubt I have been in for some time, and to find out whether anything can be known with certainty about material objects.

2. But before I ask whether the objects I conceive exist outside me, I must examine their ideas, as far as they are found in my consciousness, and see which of them are distinct and which are confused.

3. First, I distinctly imagine the quantity that the philosophers commonly call continuous. I imagine the extension in length, breadth and depth that belongs to this quantity, or rather to the object to which it is attributed. I can also count many different parts in it, and give each part all sorts of sizes, figures, positions and local motions. And finally, I can give each of these motions every degree of duration.

4. Nor do I only know these things distinctly when I consider them in this general way. With a little attention I also discover countless particular facts about figures, numbers, motion and the like. These are so evidently true, and fit my nature so well, that in discovering them I do not seem so much to learn something new as to remember what I knew before. Or it seems that I am noticing for the first time what was already in my mind, though I had not yet turned my attention to it.

5. What I find most important here is this. I discover in my mind countless ideas of certain objects. These cannot be counted as pure negations, although perhaps they have no reality beyond my thought. I did not make them up, even though it may be in my power to think of them or not. They have true and immutable natures of their own. Take the example of a triangle. Perhaps there is not, and never was, any such figure anywhere in the universe outside my thought. Still, it remains true that this figure has a certain determinate nature, form or essence, which is immutable and eternal, was not made up by me, and does not depend at all on my thought. This is clear from the fact that many properties of the triangle can be demonstrated: that its three angles are equal to two right angles, that its greatest side is opposite its greatest angle, and the like. Whether I wish it or not, I now clearly discern that these belong to the triangle, although I did not think of them at all when I first imagined it. So it cannot be said that I invented them.

6. It is also not a valid objection to say that this idea of a triangle perhaps came into my mind through the senses, because I have seen bodies of triangular figure. For I can form in thought countless other figures that could never have been objects of sense. Yet I can demonstrate many properties of their nature, just as I can for the triangle. All of these are assuredly true, since I clearly conceive them. They are therefore something, and not mere negations. For it is highly evident that all that is true is something, [truth being identical with existence]. And I have already shown at length that whatever is clearly and distinctly known is true. Even if this had not been demonstrated, the nature of my mind is such that I cannot help assenting to what I clearly conceive, at the time I conceive it. I also remember that even when I was still strongly attached to the objects of sense, I counted among the most certain truths those I clearly conceived about figures, numbers and other matters of arithmetic and geometry, and in general of pure mathematics.

7. Now suppose that, because I can draw the idea of an object from my thought, it follows that everything I clearly and distinctly apprehend as belonging to this object does in truth belong to it. May I not derive from this an argument for the existence of God? It is certain that I find the idea of a God in my consciousness, that is, the idea of a being supremely perfect, just as I find the idea of any figure or number. And I know just as clearly and distinctly that an [actual and] eternal existence belongs to his nature, as I know that everything demonstrable of a figure or number really belongs to the nature of that figure or number. Therefore, even if all the conclusions of the preceding Meditations were false, the existence of God would count for me as a truth at least as certain as any truth of mathematics I have ever judged.

8. At first sight, such a doctrine may seem to contain more sophistry than truth. In every other matter I have been accustomed to distinguish existence from essence, so I easily believe that existence can be separated from the essence of God, and that God can thus be conceived as not actually existing. But when I think about it more attentively, it appears that existence can no more be separated from the essence of God than the idea of a mountain can be separated from that of a valley, or than the equality of its three angles to two right angles can be separated from the essence of a [rectilinear] triangle. So it is no less impossible to conceive a God, that is, a being supremely perfect, who lacks existence, or who is devoid of some perfection, than to conceive a mountain without a valley.

9. Still, I cannot conceive a God except as existing, any more than I can conceive a mountain without a valley. But it does not follow that there is any mountain in the world merely because I conceive a mountain with a valley. In the same way, although I conceive God as existing, it does not seem to follow that God exists. For my thought imposes no necessity on things. I may imagine a winged horse although there is none, and so perhaps I could attribute existence to God although no God existed.

10. But the cases are not analogous, and a fallacy lies hidden under the appearance of this objection. From the fact that I cannot conceive a mountain without a valley, it does not follow that any mountain or valley exists. It follows only that the mountain and the valley, whether or not they exist, are inseparable from each other. On the other hand, from the fact that I cannot conceive God except as existing, it follows that existence is inseparable from him, and therefore that he really exists. This is not brought about by my thought, and my thought imposes no necessity on things. On the contrary, the necessity that lies in the thing itself, that is, the necessity of the existence of God, determines me to think in this way. For I am not free to conceive a God without existence, that is, a being supremely perfect yet devoid of an absolute perfection, as I am free to imagine a horse with or without wings.

11. Nor should anyone object here that, once I have supposed God to have all perfections, I must indeed admit that he exists, since existence is one of them, but that my original supposition was not necessary. In the same way, it is not necessary to think that all quadrilateral figures can be inscribed in a circle. For if I supposed this, I would be forced to admit that the rhombus, a figure of four sides, can be inscribed in it, which is manifestly false. This objection, I say, is not competent. It may not be necessary that I ever entertain the notion of Deity. Yet each time I happen to think of a first and supreme being, and to draw the idea of him, so to speak, from the storehouse of the mind, I am compelled to attribute to him all kinds of perfections, though I may not then list them all or think of each one in particular. And this necessity is enough, as soon as I discover that existence is a perfection, to make me infer the existence of this first and supreme being. Likewise, it is not necessary that I ever imagine any triangle. But whenever I wish to consider a rectilinear figure made of only three angles, I must attribute to it those properties from which it is correctly inferred that its three angles are not greater than two right angles, even if perhaps I do not then notice this relation in particular. But when I consider which figures can be inscribed in a circle, it is by no means necessary to hold that all quadrilateral figures are among them. On the contrary, I cannot even imagine this to be so, as long as I am unwilling to accept in thought anything that I do not clearly and distinctly conceive. Consequently there is a vast difference between false suppositions, like the one in question, and the true ideas that were born with me, the first and chief of which is the idea of God. For I discern on many grounds that this idea is not factitious, depending simply on my thought, but that it is the representation of a true and immutable nature. First, I can conceive no other being, except God, to whose essence existence [necessarily] belongs. Second, it is impossible to conceive two or more gods of this kind. And supposing that one such God exists, I clearly see that he must have existed from all eternity and will exist to all eternity. Finally, I apprehend many other properties in God, none of which I can diminish or change.

12. But whatever method of proof I finally adopt, it always comes back to this: only the things I clearly and distinctly conceive have the power to persuade me completely. Of the objects I conceive in this way, some are obvious to everyone, while others are discovered only after close and careful investigation. Nevertheless, once they are discovered, the latter are not thought less certain than the former. Take a right-angled triangle. It is not as manifest at first that the square of the base is equal to the squares of the other two sides as it is that the base is opposite the greatest angle. Nevertheless, once it is apprehended, we are as firmly persuaded of the truth of the former as of the latter. And as for God, if I were not preoccupied by prejudices, and if my thought were not beset on all sides by the constant presence of the images of sensible objects, I would know nothing sooner or more easily than the fact of his being. For is there any truth clearer than the existence of a Supreme Being, or of God, since it is to his essence alone that [necessary and eternal] existence belongs?

13. It has cost me much close thinking to conceive this truth rightly. Nevertheless, I now feel not only as assured of it as of what I deem most certain, but I also remark that the certitude of all other truths depends so absolutely on it that without this knowledge it is impossible ever to know anything perfectly.

14. I am so made that, while I have a very clear and distinct apprehension of a matter, I cannot resist the conviction that it is true. But my constitution is also such that I cannot keep my mind continually fixed on the same object. And I often recall a past judgment without being able to recall its grounds at the same time. So it may happen, meanwhile, that other reasons are presented to me that would readily make me change my opinion, if I did not know that God existed. Thus I would have no true and certain knowledge, but only vague and shifting opinions. For example, when I consider the nature of the [rectilinear] triangle, it appears to me most clearly, since I have been instructed in the principles of geometry, that its three angles are equal to two right angles. And while I apply my mind to the demonstration, I find it impossible to believe otherwise. But as soon as I stop attending to the process of proof, I may readily come to doubt the truth demonstrated, if I do not know that there is a God, even though I still remember that I had a clear comprehension of it. For I may persuade myself that nature has so constituted me that I am sometimes deceived, even in matters that I think I apprehend with the greatest evidence and certitude. This is especially so when I recall that I often considered many things true and certain which other reasons afterward forced me to count as wholly false.

15. But I have now discovered that God exists. At the same time I observed that all things depend on him and that he is no deceiver, and I inferred from this that all that I clearly and distinctly perceive is of necessity true. So although I no longer attend to the grounds of a judgment, no opposing reason can be alleged that is sufficient to lead me to doubt its truth, provided only that I remember that I once had a clear and distinct comprehension of it. My knowledge of it thus becomes true and certain. This same knowledge extends to whatever I remember having demonstrated earlier, such as the truths of geometry and the like. For what can be alleged against them to lead me to doubt them? Will it be that my nature is such that I may often be deceived? But I already know that I cannot be deceived in judgments whose grounds I clearly know. Will it be that I formerly deemed things true and certain which I afterward discovered to be false? But I had no clear and distinct knowledge of any of those things. I was still ignorant of the rule by which I am assured of the truth of a judgment, and I was led to assent to them on grounds that I afterward discovered were weaker than I had imagined at the time. What further objection, then, is there? Will it be said that perhaps I am dreaming (an objection I raised myself a short while ago), or that all the thoughts I am now conscious of have no more truth than the reveries of my dreams? Even if I were in truth dreaming, the rule still holds that all that is clearly presented to my intellect is indisputably true.

16. And so I see very clearly that the certitude and truth of all science depends on the knowledge of the true God alone. Before I knew him, I could have no perfect knowledge of anything else. Now that I know him, I have the means of acquiring perfect knowledge about countless matters, both about God himself and other intellectual objects, and about corporeal nature, in so far as it is the object of pure mathematics [which do not consider whether it exists or not].

chapters.title: Meditation 6 — Of the Existence of Material Things, and of the Real Distinction Between the Mind and Body of Man
paragraphs: 1. It now remains only to inquire whether material things exist. On this question I know at least this with certainty: such things may exist, insofar as they are the object of pure mathematics, because when I regard them in that aspect I can conceive them clearly and distinctly. There can be no doubt that God has the power to produce everything I am able to conceive distinctly, and I have never judged anything impossible for him unless I found a contradiction in trying to conceive it aright. Further, I have a faculty of imagination, and I am conscious of using it whenever I apply myself to considering material things. This is enough to persuade me that they exist. For when I attentively consider what imagination is, I find that it is simply a certain application of the cognitive faculty (facultas cognoscitiva) to a body that is immediately present to it, and which therefore exists.

2. To make this quite clear, I first remark the difference between imagination and pure intellection [or conception]. When I imagine a triangle, for example, I not only conceive (intelligo) that it is a figure bounded by three lines; at the same time I look upon (intueor) those three lines as present, by the power and internal application of my mind (acie mentis). This is what I call imagining. Suppose instead that I want to think of a chiliogon. I rightly conceive that it is a figure made of a thousand sides, just as easily as I conceive that a triangle is a figure made of only three. But I cannot imagine the thousand sides of a chiliogon as I do the three sides of a triangle, nor, so to speak, view them as present [with the eyes of my mind]. Now I have the habit of always imagining something when I think of corporeal things. So when I conceive a chiliogon, it may happen that I confusedly represent some figure to myself. Yet it is quite evident that this figure is not a chiliogon, since it in no way differs from the one I would represent if I were thinking of a myriogon or any other many-sided figure. Nor would this representation help at all in discovering and unfolding the properties that make a chiliogon differ from other polygons. But if the question is about a pentagon, it is quite true that I can conceive its figure, as I can that of a chiliogon, without the aid of imagination. I can also imagine it, however, by applying the attention of my mind to its five sides and at the same time to the area they enclose. Thus I observe that imagining requires a special effort of mind that conceiving or understanding (ad intelligendum) does not require; and this special exertion of mind clearly shows the difference between imagination and pure intellection (imaginatio et intellectio pura).

3. I remark, besides, that this power of imagination which I possess, insofar as it differs from the power of conceiving, is in no way necessary to my [nature or] essence, that is, to the essence of my mind. For even if I did not have it, I should still remain the same as I now am; from which it seems we may conclude that it depends on something different from the mind. And I easily understand that if some body exists to which my mind is so conjoined and united that it can, as it were, consider it whenever it chooses, then the mind may in this way imagine corporeal objects. On this view, this mode of thinking differs from pure intellection only in that, in conceiving, the mind turns in some way upon itself and considers one of the ideas it has within itself; but in imagining, it turns toward the body and contemplates in it some object that conforms to an idea, which the mind either conceived by itself or apprehended by sense. I say I easily understand that imagination may be formed in this way, if it is true that there are bodies. And because I find no other obvious way of explaining it, I conjecture from this, with probability, that bodies exist — but only with probability. Although I examine everything carefully, I still do not find that I can necessarily infer the existence of any body from the distinct idea of corporeal nature that I have in my imagination.

4. But I am accustomed to imagine many other objects besides that corporeal nature which is the object of pure mathematics — colors, sounds, tastes, pain and the like, for example — although less distinctly. I perceive these much better by the senses, and it is through the senses and memory that they seem to have reached the imagination. So I believe that, to examine them to better advantage, I should at the same time examine what sense-perception is. I should inquire whether the ideas apprehended by this mode of thinking (consciousness) can give me a certain proof of the existence of corporeal objects.

5. First, I will recall to my mind the things I have until now held to be true because I perceived them by the senses, and the foundations on which my belief in their truth rested. Second, I will examine the reasons that afterward forced me to doubt them. Finally, I will consider what I ought now to believe about them.

6. First, then, I perceived that I had a head, hands, feet and other members making up that body, which I considered a part, or perhaps even the whole, of myself. I perceived further that this body was placed among many others, by which it could be affected in various ways, beneficial and hurtful. I noticed what was beneficial by a certain sensation of pleasure, and what was hurtful by a sensation of pain. Besides pleasure and pain, I was also conscious of hunger, thirst and other appetites, and of certain corporeal inclinations toward joy, sadness, anger and similar passions. Outside myself, besides the extension, figure and motions of bodies, I also perceived in them hardness, heat and the other tactile qualities, and in addition light, colors, odors, tastes and sounds. The variety of these let me tell the sky, the earth, the sea, and generally all other bodies apart from one another. And certainly, considering the ideas of all these qualities, which were presented to my mind and which alone I properly and immediately perceived, I had reason to think I perceived certain objects wholly different from my thought, namely bodies from which those ideas proceeded. For I was conscious that the ideas came to me without my consent being required: I could not perceive any object, however much I wished to, unless it was present to the organ of sense; and when it was present, I could not possibly fail to perceive it. Also, the ideas I perceived by the senses were much more lively and clear, and even, in their own way, more distinct than any I could frame myself by meditation or found impressed on my memory. So it seemed they could not have proceeded from myself, and must therefore have been caused in me by some other objects. And since I had no knowledge of those objects beyond what the ideas themselves gave me, the supposition most likely to occur to my mind was that the objects were similar to the ideas they caused. I also recollected that I had formerly trusted the senses rather than reason, that the ideas I formed myself were not so clear as those I perceived by sense, and that they were even for the most part composed of parts of the latter. So I was readily persuaded that I had no idea in my intellect that had not formerly passed through the senses. Nor was I altogether wrong to believe that the body which, by a special right, I called my own, pertained to me more properly and strictly than any other. For I could never be separated from it as from other bodies; I felt all my appetites and affections in it and on account of it; and in fine I was affected by pain and the titillation of pleasure in its parts, and not in the parts of other bodies separated from it. But I inquired why sadness of mind should follow from this I know not what sensation of pain, and why joy should arise from the sensation of pleasure; or why this indescribable twitching of the stomach, which I call hunger, should put me in mind of taking food, and the parchedness of the throat of drink, and so in other cases. I was unable to give any explanation, except that I was so taught by nature. For there is assuredly no affinity, at least none I can comprehend, between this irritation of the stomach and the desire for food, any more than between the perception of an object that causes pain and the consciousness of sadness that springs from the perception. In the same way it seemed to me that all the other judgments I had formed about the objects of sense were dictates of nature, because I remarked that I formed those judgments before I had leisure to weigh and consider the reasons that might constrain me to form them.

7. But afterward a wide experience gradually undermined the faith I had placed in my senses. I frequently observed that towers which seemed round at a distance looked square when viewed more closely, and that colossal figures raised on the summits of those towers looked like small statues when seen from the bottom. In other instances without number I also found error in judgments based on the external senses. And not only in those based on the external senses, but even in those resting on the internal senses; for is there anything more internal than pain? Yet I have sometimes been told by people whose arm or leg had been amputated that they still occasionally seemed to feel pain in the part of the body they had lost. This led me to think that I could not be quite certain even that any one of my members was affected when I felt pain in it. Shortly afterward I added two other grounds of doubt, of very wide generality. The first was that I believed I never perceived anything when awake that I could not occasionally think I also perceived when asleep; and since I do not believe that the ideas I seem to perceive in sleep proceed from objects external to me, I saw no more ground for believing this of the ideas I seem to perceive when awake. The second was that I was as yet ignorant of the author of my being, or at least supposed myself to be; so I saw nothing to prevent my having been so constituted by nature that I should be deceived even in matters that appeared to me most true. As for the grounds on which I had before been persuaded of the existence of sensible objects, I had no great difficulty finding suitable answers. Nature seemed to incline me to many things from which reason made me averse, so I thought I ought not to put much confidence in its teachings. And although the perceptions of the senses did not depend on my will, I did not think I should conclude on that ground that they proceeded from things different from myself, since perhaps there might be found in me some faculty, though hitherto unknown to me, which produced them.

8. But now I begin to know myself better and to discover more clearly the author of my being. I do not, indeed, think I should rashly admit everything the senses seem to teach; nor, on the other hand, am I convinced that I should doubt their teachings in general.

9. Here is the first point. I know that God can produce everything I clearly and distinctly conceive, exactly as I conceive it. So if I can clearly and distinctly conceive one thing apart from another, that alone makes me certain the two are different: God's omnipotence could at least make them exist separately. It does not matter what power would bring about the separation; I am still compelled to judge them different. Now I know with certitude that I exist, and meanwhile I observe nothing else that necessarily belongs to my nature or essence except that I am a thinking thing. I therefore rightly conclude that my essence consists only in being a thinking thing [or a substance whose whole essence or nature is merely thinking]. I may indeed possess a body to which I am very closely conjoined — or rather, as I will shortly say, I certainly do. Nevertheless I have a clear and distinct idea of myself as only a thinking and unextended thing. And I also have a distinct idea of body as only an extended and unthinking thing. So it is certain that I, [that is, my mind, by which I am what I am], am entirely and truly distinct from my body, and can exist without it.

10. I find in myself, moreover, several faculties of thinking, each with its own special mode. I find, for example, the faculties of imagining and perceiving. I can indeed clearly and distinctly conceive myself as a whole without them. But I cannot conceive them without conceiving myself; that is, they require an intelligent substance in which they reside. For [in the notion we have of them, or to use the terms of the schools] their formal concept includes some sort of intellection. Hence I perceive that they are distinct from myself, as modes are from things. I notice certain other faculties too, such as changing place or taking on various figures. Like the preceding ones, these cannot be conceived, and so cannot exist, apart from a substance in which they inhere. It is very evident, however, that if these faculties really exist, they must belong to some corporeal or extended substance; for their clear and distinct concept contains some sort of extension, and no intellection at all. Further, I cannot doubt that I have a certain passive faculty of perception, that is, of receiving and recognizing the ideas of sensible things. But this would be useless to me unless there were also an active faculty, in me or in something else, able to form and produce those ideas. Yet this active faculty cannot be in me [insofar as I am but a thinking thing], seeing that it does not presuppose thought, and also that those ideas are often produced in my mind without any contribution from me, and even often against my will. So this faculty must exist in a substance different from me. In that substance, as I remarked before, all the objective reality of the ideas it produces is contained formally or eminently. This substance is either a body, that is, a corporeal nature that contains formally [and in effect] everything contained objectively [and by representation] in those ideas; or it is God Himself, or some other creature of a rank superior to body, that contains the same eminently. But God is no deceiver. So it is manifest that He does not send me those ideas directly from Himself, nor through any creature that contains their objective reality not formally but only eminently. For He has given me no faculty to discover that this is so. On the contrary, He has given me a very strong inclination to believe that the ideas arise from corporeal objects. I do not see how He could be cleared of deceit if they really came from some other source or were produced by other causes than corporeal things. Accordingly, it must be concluded that corporeal objects exist. They are perhaps not exactly as we perceive them by the senses, since sense perception is in many cases very obscure and confused. But at least we must admit that everything I clearly and distinctly conceive in them, that is, generally speaking everything included in the object of speculative geometry, really exists external to me.

11. Other things are merely particular, such as that the sun has such a size and figure, etc.; or they are conceived with less clearness and distinctness, such as light, sound, pain and the like. These are highly dubious and uncertain. Nevertheless, God is no deceiver, and so he has not allowed any falsity in my opinions without also giving me a faculty to correct it. On that ground alone I think I may safely conclude that I have in myself the means of arriving at the truth. And first, it cannot be doubted that every dictate of nature contains some truth. For by nature, taken in general, I now understand nothing other than God Himself, or the order and arrangement God established in created things. By my own nature in particular I understand everything God has given me.

12. But there is nothing that nature teaches me more expressly [or more sensibly] than this: I have a body, which is ill affected when I feel pain, and which needs food and drink when I feel hunger and thirst, etc. So I ought not to doubt that there is some truth in this information.

13. Nature also teaches me, through these sensations of pain, hunger, thirst, etc., that I am not merely lodged in my body like a pilot in a ship. I am so closely joined to it, and as it were mingled with it, that mind and body make up one unity. Otherwise, since I am merely a thinking thing, I should not feel pain when my body is hurt. I should perceive the wound by the understanding alone, as a pilot sees by sight that some part of his ship is damaged. And when my body needed food or drink, I should know it clearly, instead of being told by the confused sensations of hunger and thirst. For in truth these sensations of hunger, thirst, pain, etc., are nothing but certain confused modes of thinking, which arise from the union, and apparent fusion, of mind and body.

14. Nature teaches me, besides, that many other bodies surround my own, and that I must seek some of them and shun others. I perceive different kinds of colors, sounds, odors, tastes, heat, hardness, etc. From this I safely conclude that the bodies from which these various perceptions of the senses come have certain corresponding varieties, though perhaps these are not really like the perceptions. And some of these perceptions are agreeable and others disagreeable. So there can be no doubt that surrounding bodies may affect my body, or rather my whole self insofar as I am composed of body and mind, in different ways, both beneficial and harmful.

15. There are, however, many other beliefs that seem to be taught by nature but are not. They found a place in my mind through a habit of judging things without enough consideration, and such judgments can easily contain error. Here are examples. I hold that any space where nothing affects [or makes an impression on] my senses is void. I hold that a hot body contains something in every respect similar to my idea of heat; that a white or green body contains the very whiteness or greenness I perceive; that a bitter or sweet body contains the same taste, and so on; and that the stars, towers and all distant bodies have the same size and figure as they appear to have to our eyes, etc. To avoid any indistinctness of conception, I must define precisely what I properly mean by being taught by nature. I am using nature here in a narrower sense than the sum of all that God has given me. In that wider sense the notion takes in much that belongs only to the mind [which I am not referring to here when I use the term nature]: for example, my notion of the truth that what is done cannot be undone, and all the other truths I discern by the natural light [ without the aid of the body]. It also takes in much that belongs only to body and is not included here under the name nature, such as the quality of heaviness and the like, of which I am not speaking. I keep the term exclusively for the things God has given me as a being composed of mind and body. In the sense I have explained, then, nature teaches me to shun whatever causes me the sensation of pain, and to pursue whatever gives me the sensation of pleasure, and other things of that sort. I do not find, however, that it also teaches me to draw conclusions about external objects from these diverse perceptions of the senses, unless the mind has first considered them [carefully and maturely]. For, as it appears to me, discerning the truth in such matters is the task of the mind alone, not of the composite whole of mind and body. Thus a star makes no larger an impression on my eye than the flame of a candle does. Yet I feel no real or positive impulse that determines me to believe the star is not greater than the flame. The true account is merely that I have judged so since my youth, without any rational ground. Likewise I feel heat when I approach the fire, and pain if I come too close. But this gives me no ground for holding that something resembling the heat I feel is in the fire, any more than that something similar to the pain is in it. All I have ground for believing is that the fire contains something, whatever it may be, which excites in me those sensations of heat or pain. In the same way, there are spaces where I find nothing that excites and affects my senses; but I must not therefore conclude that those spaces contain no body. For I see that here, as in many similar matters, I have been accustomed to pervert the order of nature. Nature gave me the perceptions of the senses merely to signify to my mind what is beneficial and what is hurtful to the composite whole of which it is a part, and they are clear and distinct enough for that purpose. Nevertheless I use them as infallible rules for determining at once the essence of the bodies outside me, about which they can of course give me only the most obscure and confused knowledge.

16. I have already considered sufficiently how falsity can arise in my judgments despite the supreme goodness of God. A difficulty remains, however, concerning the things nature teaches me to pursue or avoid, and concerning the internal sensations, in which I seem sometimes to have detected error, [and so to be directly deceived by nature]. Suppose, for example, that some viand tastes agreeable, but poison has been mixed into it; the taste may deceive me into taking the poison. In this case, however, nature may be excused. It leads me only to desire the viand for its agreeable taste, not the poison, which nature does not know about. All we can infer from this is that our nature is not omniscient. There is certainly no ground for surprise at that: man has a finite nature, so his knowledge must be of limited perfection.

17. But we also fairly often err in what nature directly impels us to, as sick people do when they long for drink or food that would harm them. Perhaps it will be objected that such people are deceived because their nature is corrupted. That does not remove the difficulty, for a sick man is just as truly a creature of God as a healthy man, so it is equally repugnant to the goodness of God that the former's nature should be deceitful as that the latter's should be. Take a clock, made of wheels and counter weights. If it is badly made and tells the hours wrongly, it follows all the laws of nature just as accurately as when it does exactly what its maker wanted. Likewise, consider the human body as a sort of machine, built and put together from bones, nerves, muscles, veins, blood and skin. Suppose that even if it had no mind in it, it would still make all the same motions it now makes involuntarily, and so without the aid of the mind, [simply through the dispositions of its organs]. I easily see that such a body, if it were dropsical, for example, would naturally experience the parchedness of throat that is usually joined in the mind with the sensation of thirst. This parchedness would dispose it to move its nerves and other parts as drinking requires, so that it would worsen its illness and harm itself. And it is just as natural for a body that is not ill to be moved to drink for its own good by a similar cause. Now, with regard to the use its maker intended a clock for, I may say that it departs from its proper nature when it tells the hours wrongly. On the same principle, if I regard the machine of the human body as formed by God for the sake of the motions it usually shows, I may likewise have ground to think that it departs from the order of its nature when the throat is parched and drink does not help to preserve it. Nevertheless I plainly see that this second sense of the term nature is very different from the first. The second is nothing more than a certain denomination, which depends entirely on my thought, and is therefore called extrinsic: by it I compare a sick man and an imperfectly built clock with the idea I have of a healthy man and a well made clock. The first sense of nature means something truly found in things, and so having some truth.

18. But certainly, in the case of a dropsical body, it is only by exterior denomination that we say its nature is corrupted when its throat is parched and yet it does not need drink. In the case of the composite whole, however, that is, the mind united with the body, it is not a mere denomination: it is really an error of nature that it feels thirst when drink would harm it. And so it still remains to consider why the goodness of God does not keep the nature of man, taken in this way, from being fallacious.

19. To begin this examination, I first observe that mind and body differ vastly in this respect: body, by its nature, is always divisible, while mind is entirely indivisible. For when I consider the mind, that is, when I consider myself only as a thinking thing, I can distinguish no parts in myself. I discern very clearly that I am something absolutely one and entire. The whole mind seems to be united to the whole body; yet when a foot, an arm or any other part is cut off, I am conscious that nothing has been taken away from my mind. Nor can the faculties of willing, perceiving, conceiving and so on properly be called parts of it, since it is one and the same mind that is exercised [all entire] in willing, in perceiving and in conceiving. With corporeal or extended things the very opposite holds. I cannot imagine any of them [however small] that I cannot easily divide in thought, and so I know it to be divisible. This alone would be enough to teach me that the mind, or soul, of man is entirely different from the body, if I had not already learned it on other grounds.

20. I observe next that the mind does not receive impressions directly from all the parts of the body. It receives them only from the brain, or perhaps even from one small part of it, namely the part where the common sense (senses communis) is said to reside. Each time this part is affected in the same way, it produces the same perception in the mind, even though the other parts of the body may meanwhile be in different conditions. Innumerable experiments prove this, and there is no need to list them here.

21. I observe, besides, that body is of such a nature that when one of its parts is moved by another part some distance away, it can be moved in the same way by any of the parts lying between the two, even though the most remote part does nothing at all. Take, for example, a cord A, B, C, D [held in tension]. If its last part D is pulled, the first part A will move no differently than it would if B or C, one of the intermediate parts, were pulled while D stayed fixed. In the same way, when I feel pain in the foot, the science of physics teaches me how the sensation comes about. Nerves are spread through the foot and run from it to the brain like cords. When they are drawn tight in the foot, they draw tight at the same time the inmost parts of the brain where they originate, and they excite in those parts a certain motion that nature has appointed to cause in the mind a sensation of pain, as if it were in the foot. But these nerves must pass through the tibia, the leg, the loins, the back and the neck to reach the brain. So it may happen that their extremities in the foot are not affected, and only some of their parts in the loins or neck are, and yet this motion excites in the brain the same movements that an injury to the foot would have caused there. The mind will then necessarily feel pain in the foot, just as if the foot had been hurt. The same is true of all the other perceptions of our senses.

22. I observe, finally, that each movement made in the part of the brain that immediately affects the mind impresses it with only a single sensation. So the most likely supposition is that this movement makes the mind experience, out of all the sensations it could produce, the one best fitted, and generally most useful, for preserving the human body in full health. But experience shows that all the perceptions nature has given us are of just this kind. Accordingly, nothing is found in them that does not show the power and goodness of God. Thus, for example, when the nerves of the foot are shaken violently or more than usual, the motion passes through the medulla of the spine to the innermost parts of the brain. There it gives the mind a sign on which it experiences a sensation, namely of pain, as if in the foot. By this the mind is warned and urged to do its utmost to remove the cause, as dangerous and harmful to the foot. It is true that God could have constituted the nature of man so that the same motion in the brain would have informed the mind of something altogether different. The motion might, for example, have been the occasion on which the mind became conscious of itself as it is in the brain, or as it is in some place intermediate between the foot and the brain, or, finally, the occasion on which it perceived some quite different object, whatever that might be. But none of this would have contributed so well to the preservation of the body as what the mind actually feels. In the same way, when we need drink, a certain dryness arises in the throat from this want. It moves the throat's nerves, and through them the internal parts of the brain. This movement affects the mind with the sensation of thirst, because on that occasion nothing is more useful to us than to be made aware that we need drink to preserve our health. So it is in other instances.

23. From this it is quite manifest that, despite the supreme goodness of God, the nature of man, insofar as it is composed of mind and body, cannot but be sometimes fallacious. For suppose some cause excites, not in the foot but in one of the parts of the nerves stretching from the foot to the brain, or even in the brain itself, the same movement that is ordinarily produced when the foot is injured. Then pain will be felt as if in the foot, and the sense will thus be naturally deceived. For the same movement in the brain can impress the mind only with the same sensation, and this sensation is far more often excited by a cause that hurts the foot than by one acting elsewhere. So it is reasonable that the movement should lead the mind to feel pain in the foot rather than in any other part of the body. Again, the dryness of the throat sometimes does not arise, as it usually does, from the body's need of drink for its health, but from quite the opposite cause, as happens with the dropsical. Even so, it is much better that the sensation should be deceitful in that instance than that it should be continually fallacious when the body is in good condition. The same holds in other cases.

24. And certainly this consideration is of great service. It enables me to recognize the errors to which my nature is liable, and it also makes them easier to avoid or correct. For I know that all my senses more often indicate what is true than what is false in matters relating to the advantage of the body. I can almost always use more than one sense to examine the same object. Besides this, I can use my memory to connect present knowledge with past, and I have my understanding, which has already discovered all the causes of my errors. So I ought no longer to fear that falsity may be found in what the senses present to me every day. And I ought to reject all the doubts of those earlier days as hyperbolical and ridiculous, especially the general uncertainty about sleep, which I could not distinguish from the waking state. For I now find a very marked difference between the two. Our memory can never connect our dreams with one another and with the course of life, as it habitually does with events that occur while we are awake. Indeed, suppose someone appeared to me while I was awake, all of a sudden, and disappeared just as suddenly, as the images I see in sleep do, so that I could not observe where he came from or where he went. I should not without reason consider him a specter or phantom formed in my brain, rather than a real man. But there are objects for which I can determine distinctly the place they come from, the place where they are, and the time at which they appear to me. And I can connect my perception of them, without interruption, with all the other parts of my life. Then I am perfectly sure that I perceive them while I am awake and not in sleep. I ought not to doubt the truth of these presentations in the least, if I have called together all my senses, my memory and my understanding to examine them, and none of these faculties gives a report that conflicts with that of any other. For since God is no deceiver, it necessarily follows that I am not deceived in this. But the necessities of action often oblige us to decide before we have had time for so careful an examination. So it must be confessed that the life of man is often liable to error about individual objects; and we must, in conclusion, acknowledge the weakness of our nature.
